chapters.summary: Council staff opens the hearing, asks attendees to silence devices, reminds them not to approach the dais, and invites Chair Schulman to begin.
chapters.title: Hearing called to order and housekeeping announcements

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Health.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, ladies and gentlemen, we please ask that you silence all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to fill out a testimony slip, then please see one of the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Approaching the front dais is strictly prohibited.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, please do not approach the front dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lynn Schulman opens the hearing on NYC's response to the 2026 Upper East Side Legionnaires' cluster that sickened 94, hospitalized 79, and killed 11. She thanks Speaker Menin for her leadership and turns to the Speaker for remarks.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman introduces oversight hearing on 2026 Legionnaires' disease cluster

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Lynn Schulman, Chair of the New York City Council's Committee on Health.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you all for joining us at today's hearing on New York City's response to the 2026 Legionnaires Disease Cluster.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: At this hearing, we will examine the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene's response to this year's cluster in the Upper East Side of Manhattan, which sickened 94 people, of whom 79 were hospitalized.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We lost 11 New Yorkers to this year's outbreak, making this the deadliest Legionnaires outbreak in our city since 2015.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We grieve for the lives lost and we send strength to their families and loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank Speaker Julie-Menin for being here today and for her steadfast leadership on this issue as she advocated for her district and for all New Yorkers, demanding action and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to the Speaker for her remarks.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin commends DOHMH staff but questions whether NYC was adequately prepared, noting only 35 of 56 authorized water ecologist positions were staffed during the outbreak and calling for a clear accounting of vacancies.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin addresses preparedness failures and staffing vacancies before outbreak

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I first of all want to thank Chair Shulman for convening this very important hearing and all of our colleagues who are here today and members of the public.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And thank you to the Department of Health for being here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We look forward to it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to hearing your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So this summer, as we all know, Legionnaire's disease outbreak has hit incredibly close to home for many of us.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It occurred in the district that I represent and took the lives of 11 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our hearts break for their family members and we send them our deepest, deepest condolences.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These are our neighbors, they are our friends and our loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I have certainly experienced this public health crisis not only as an elected official, but as a New Yorker representing constituents directly affected by the city's response.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to be very clear from the outset.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We first of all want to commend the health department staff who worked tirelessly to investigate this outbreak, inspect and test cooling towers, conduct outreach, and protect New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These hardworking public servants deserve our respect.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But today's hearing must also ask a fundamental question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Was New York City adequately prepared before this outbreak occurred?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Legionnaire's disease is not a new threat.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know it occurs in New York City every year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know cooling towers require rigorous inspection and oversight.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we knew before this outbreak that the health department needed additional staff to do this work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yet during the outbreak, only 35 of 56 authorized water ecologist positions were staffed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That means 21 authorized positions were not yet staffed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: with active inspectors when the city needed this specialized workforce the most.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Water ecologists perform critical work inspecting cooling towers and other water systems, identifying potential hazards, enforcing regulations, and helping prevent

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: outbreaks.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin raises concerns about whether inspection and enforcement increased ahead of summer months, noting new cooling tower testing requirements took effect in May and questioning whether building owners were identified and held accountable proactively.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin on enforcement gaps and cooling tower compliance before summer

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There are also serious questions about vacancies within the health department's broader inspection workforce and that is one of the many series of questions that we will get to today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today we need a clear accounting of how many water ecologists and public health inspector positions were budgeted, filled, vacant, and occupied by employees who were still onboarding or training when this outbreak occurred.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If Legionnaire's disease is a recurring public health threat, which we know it is, we should not be scrambling to build the workforce needed to address it after an outbreak has already started.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We should have been prepared.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Preparedness also means ensuring that our cooling tower laws are actually being enforced.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This past May, New York City experienced temperatures approaching 100 degrees, unusually early in the season.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New cooling tower testing requirements had also just taken effect.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We need to understand whether inspection and enforcement increased accordingly,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: whether building owners who failed to comply were quickly identified, and whether the department had enough staff to proactively enforce these requirements.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin describes constituents who didn't know symptoms, vulnerability factors, or precautions, and cites conflicting guidance at Haven Plaza about showering. She calls for clear, consistent, repeated public guidance before the next outbreak.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin on public communication failures during outbreak

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There's another

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: area where we must do better, and that is making sure New Yorkers understand exactly what they should do when Legionnaire's disease is detected in their community.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I do not want to suggest that the health department did not communicate.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The department conducted outreach and distributed information, but communication is only successful if people understand the risk and know what actions they need to take.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Throughout this outbreak, I heard repeatedly from constituents who did not know the symptoms of Legionnaire's disease, who was most vulnerable, when they should seek medical attention, or what they could do to proactively protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Residents also had basic questions about whether it was safe to shower, drink tap water, or use their air conditioners.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We saw just how confusing public guidance can become at Haven Plaza in a separate Legionella situation involving a building water system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Video and reports from that situation showed residents receiving differing messages about whether they could even shower.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: When we're dealing with a potentially deadly disease, residents should not be left trying to reconcile conflicting information themselves.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The city must provide clear, consistent, and repeated guidance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New Yorkers should know the symptoms of Legionnaire's disease before the next outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They should know who is at greater risk.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They should know when to contact a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And when an outbreak occurs, they should quickly receive clear information.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: about what precautions they should take.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin reads a powerful statement from the family of a young doctor who died July 19 after contracting Legionnaires on July 4. The family describes her as kind, funny, ambitious, and calls for accountability and policy changes to prevent future deaths.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin reads statement from family of 32-year-old pediatrician who died

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Ultimately, I want to ensure that we keep our focus today on the people who really matter, the New Yorkers who became ill and the New Yorkers whose lives were tragically cut short.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Eleven New Yorkers have died in connection with this outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will soon hear from family members who lost their loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To this horrible disease.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But before then, I want to read a statement on behalf of a family who lost their loved one.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They wanted this statement read.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They felt very strongly about this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This hearing should be about her, and it should be about all 11 New Yorkers who are no longer with us today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They deserve answers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Their families deserve answers, and they deserve for us as policymakers to determine what should have been done differently and make the changes necessary to prevent another family from experiencing this kind of loss.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I will now read the statement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My sister, a 32-year-old medical doctor with many decades of her life still ahead of her, was the fourth victim of the 2026 Upper East Side Legionnaires Disease outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Her career as a pediatrician, dedicating her life to helping children and young people, was only just beginning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My sister was enormously kind, funny, ambitious, and exceptionally intelligent.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My whole life, I looked up to her and wanted to be like her.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She cared deeply for those around her, her wife, her two younger sisters, her parents, her friends, and loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: loved ones, as well as a patient she treated who described her as incredibly compassionate.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My sister had so much life left to live.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Instead, she became critically ill and was admitted to the ICU with Legionnaire's disease on the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because of her autoimmune condition, my sister was particularly vigilant about protecting her health.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She took all necessary precautions and followed all health guidance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: However, she was not prepared for an invisible threat in her own home, the one place where she was meant to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My sister developed symptoms two to three days before she was admitted to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: By this time, a cluster of Legionnaires cases had already been identified, but not yet widely communicated to the local residents, including those who were known to be at greater risk.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Had she been better informed and known about the risk and early symptoms, she could have been evaluated sooner and started on life-saving antibiotics earlier.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will never know whether the outcome would have been different.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My sister was admitted to the ICU, experienced an emergency intubation, and fought for her life for over two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She endured an unimaginable amount of invasive medical treatments and attempts to save her life.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Despite all these efforts, my sister died on the 19th of July 2026, surrounded by her family, her wife, and loved ones.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We remain devastated.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There are no adequate words to describe our loss.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To lose her so young in a completely preventable manner leaves us grappling with many difficult questions about the multiple failures that allowed our

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: dearest sister, daughter, wife, friend, and doctor, to die so unexpectedly and traumatically.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: My sister always believed in helping others and preventing suffering wherever she could.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She would not want any other person to die in vain.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We cannot bring my sister back, despite this being our deepest wish.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We can hope to prevent her death from becoming just another number or being treated as an unavoidable tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Her life mattered, and her death matters too.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We hope it leads to honest accountability in policy and practice changes so that no other family has to experience what we are enduring.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I will end with what I told my sister in the hospital while she died.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you for being my sister.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will love you forever.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I will now turn to Chair Shulman for her opening statement.

chapters.summary: Schulman presents data showing cooling tower inspections declined over 50% since 2017, from 5,000 annually to 2,300 in 2025. She cites $5.1 million in outstanding violation balances and 94 test reports showing hazardous Legionella levels with no cleanings performed.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on declining inspection rates and enforcement data

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Almost one year ago today, this committee held a hearing to discuss the city's response to the 2025 Legionnaires disease cluster in Harlem, which hospitalized 90 people and claimed seven lives.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Legionnaires disease is a serious type of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria, which can spread through water droplets dispersed by cooling towers, rooftop structures that contain water, and a fan as part of a centralized air cooling system for a building.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Most healthy individuals exposed to Legionella bacteria do not get sick, but individuals who are 50 years of age or older or have chronic health conditions or weakened immune systems are at an increased risk for illness and hospitalization.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When large Legionnaires outbreaks occur, it is almost always due

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: to the presence of live Legionella bacteria in cooling tower systems.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: However, I want to acknowledge that Legionella can also grow and spread within the plumbing system of a particular building.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: These systems are subject to different protocols.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We will hear about that today as well with a main focus on cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Over the past decade, amid multiple outbreaks, New York City has adopted some of the strictest standards for Legionella testing, cleaning, and remediation in the world.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Last year, the Council collaborated with DOHMH to enact my bill, Local Law 159, which requires building owners to conduct monthly, every 30 days,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Legionella testing and disinfect cooling towers when they are in operation, usually during the warm summer months when Legionella bacteria is most likely to grow and spread.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: DOHMH implemented this law in May with the promise that these requirements would help prevent the next outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And yet we are here again in the wake of another deeply traumatic and preventable tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: First, climate change has increased New York City's temperatures over the summer months, especially in the past two years, which gave rise to outbreaks in each of these years, creating a ripe atmosphere for Legionella bacteria to grow and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And just as important, the data shows that the laws we have on the books are only as strong as the administration's commitment to enforce them.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: According to open data records, the number of cooling tower systems inspected by DOHMH each year has declined by over 50% since 2007.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: from about 5,000 annually in 2017 to 2,300 in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: There's a chart with a graph on the screen, and you can see the precipitous fall in the number of inspections.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The slide displayed on the screen shows DOHMH data compiled into a line graph in a recent Gothamist report.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It shows that over the past decade, the overall number of cooling towers inspected in the first six months of each year has declined from over 3,000 in 2017 to just over 1,500 in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This, too, is a 50% decline.

chapters.summary: Schulman details that DOHMH issued zero summonses in January, March, May, and June in the cluster area, then 180 summonses to 78 buildings in July after the outbreak. She argues enforcement should not require an outbreak to trigger action.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman details enforcement data in Upper East Side cluster zip codes

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Data recently pulled from the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings indicate that building owners owed the city approximately $5.1 million in outstanding balances related to cooling tower violations citywide, including approximately $1.5 million

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: associated with violations that DOHMH classifies as public health hazards.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And according to a 2025 DOHMH report, DOHMH received 94 test reports showing potentially hazardous

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: regionella levels in cooling tower systems, and yet no cleanings or disinfections were performed by or on behalf of DOHMH pursuant to these tests.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The same report found at least 800 critical cooling tower violations and over 250 public health hazard violations citywide last year.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Tragically, none of this reporting led to aggressive enforcement prior to the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: According to DOHMH cooling tower inspection data and oath enforcement records for the three zip codes included in the 2026 Upper East Side cluster, enforcement was limited during the first six months of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: After excluding dismissed cases, DOHMH issued 20 summonses to six buildings in February and five summonses to one building in April while issuing none in January, March, May, or June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: However, once the cluster occurred in July, enforcement increased substantially.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: DOHMH issued 180 summonses to 78 buildings with a combined face value of $177,000 in fines.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: During the 2026 cluster, of the 58 buildings with cooling towers that tested positive through culture testing for Legionella, only two received violations between January 1st and June 17th.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Between June 18th and July 31st, however, 35 of the 58 buildings received a total of 71 summonses with a combined face value of $65,500.

chapters.summary: Schulman states the administration must increase enforcement 365 days a year and renew focus on prevention, arguing nobody should die from Legionnaires' disease and building owners must face strict consequences for violations.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman calls for year-round preventive enforcement

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: While the city's outreach efforts and transparency during the cluster improved from last year, much more needs to be done to make our cooling tower infrastructure safe for New Yorkers during the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The data shows that DOHMH can enforce these laws and protect New Yorkers when Legionnaire's disease is in the headlines and people are sick.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Now the agency needs to show the same level of commitment to preventive enforcement 365 days a year.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This cannot be the new norm.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Nobody should die from Legionnaire's disease in our city.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We cannot accept that we will lose more New Yorkers to this disease every year.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It is unacceptable to enforce this city's cooling tower laws only once an outbreak occurs.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This administration must increase enforcement at all times of the year, and it must renew its focus on preventive measures.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Building owners need to understand that there will be strict consequences for cutting corners and violating the law.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I said this last year, and I will say it again, it should not take a major outbreak to trigger enforcement of our laws.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: People should not have to die for building owners to face consequences.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We know this from over a decade of data.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When the city continuously enforces the law, we save lives.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As climate change makes our summers hotter and as our city ages and becomes more vulnerable to Legionnaire's disease, we must use every available avenue and resource to create a safer and healthier city.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We must also work to identify where our laws can be tightened and where we can do more to keep New Yorkers safe and informed.

chapters.summary: Schulman lists the eight pieces of legislation being heard, including bills on a Legionnaires hotline, testing sites, education and outreach, cooling tower cleaning, post-cluster analyses, a public database, annual compliance review, and shower hoses for tenants.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman outlines eight bills under consideration

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This Council remains deeply committed to strengthening our laws and protecting New Yorkers from the threat of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Today, the committee is considering eight pieces of legislation which all aim to stop the spread of Legionnaire's disease and keep New Yorkers as informed and as healthy as possible when an outbreak occurs.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank each sponsor for putting forward these proposals and for their commitment to this issue.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Before I talk about the bills, I want to mention that we've

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm joined today by Councilmember Salam, Epstein, Wong, Felder, Farias, Maloney, Wilson, Aldebal, Narcisse, and Murano on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: These bills include...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Introduction 1016 sponsored by myself, which would establish a dedicated DOHMH Legionnaires disease hotline

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: for the public to request information about Legionnaires disease outbreaks in New York City, as well as to provide hotline users with referrals to resources and medical services.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Introduction 999 by Councilmember Epstein in relation to establishing temporary

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Legionnaires disease testing sites and a digital map of testing sites.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Introductions 1005 and 1006 by Councilmember Maloney in relation to education and outreach on Legionnaires disease and cleaning requirements for cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Introductions by Councilmember Thomas Henry in relation to post cluster analyses of cooling towers associated with Legionnaires disease and establishing a public database of locations impacted by Legionella.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: An introduction by Councilmember Hanks in relation to an annual cooling tower compliance review and increased enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: An introduction 181 by Councilmember Farias in relation to requiring building owners to provide shower hoses and informational materials on Legionnaires disease to tenants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration, receiving thorough responses to the committee's questions, and discussing the proposed legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Commissioner Martin and Deputy Commissioners Howard and Schiff for being here.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you again to Speaker Menon for being here today and for your leadership.

chapters.summary: Council Member Amanda Farias explains her bill requiring building owners to provide shower hoses and informational materials within 24 hours of a confirmed Legionnaires case, drawing on experiences at Classon Point Gardens and Parkchester in her district.
chapters.title: Council Member Farias on Intro 181: shower hoses and tenant notification

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We will now move to Councilmember Amanda Farias for a brief statement on her bill.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Good morning and thank you Speaker Menon and Chair Shulman and the members of the Committee on Health.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for hearing Intro 181.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Today I have been working for years to push this legislation forward along with many others that are on the docket.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: After an outbreak in my district and many other communities of color made the clear need for a defined protocol to get information and practical protections to tenants when a confirmed case of Legionnaires disease is identified in their building.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: In 2022, residents at Class and Point Gardens were advised not to use their showers while the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene evaluated the development following two confirmed cases.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: When my office pressed for an alternative that residents could actually use during what could be a very lengthy testing process, as many were people with disabilities, older adults, and

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: needed mobility assistance, we worked with DOHMH and NYCHA to get shower hoses installed for the affected residents following the need of

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: no water vapor or steam, just water for people to use and not inconvenience their day-to-day lives as many were told they could not use their showers.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: That experience largely informed the legislation before us today.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Since then, we have continued to see this issue arise in resident

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: water systems including in Parkchester in my district where DOHMH initiated a building evaluation after multiple residents sharing a hot water system were diagnosed with Legionnaires disease.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: And after the Legionnaires cluster we saw this summer,

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: The need to strengthen every stage of the city's response remains just as relevant.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Even while DOHMH is investigating a source, directing testing, and overseeing any necessary remediation,

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: residents are still living in their homes and making decisions on how to use their water safely, or even having to purchase water to use water safely.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: When a case is confirmed in a residential building, the response has to reach the tenants in that building quickly.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: DOHMH's guidance should get to residents and they deserve to know what practical precautions are available to reduce their risk of exposure while the building response is underway.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: The 24-hour requirement in my bill ensures that once DOHMH has provided notice, building owners are equipped with standardized guidance to communicate clearly with tenants and take the immediate mitigation steps available to them.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: The shower hose provision is another practical tool alongside the health guidance that they are given.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: What we were able to coordinate with Class 10 Point Guardage should be built into the response when these circumstances arise.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Residents should not have to wait for an elected office, a building manager, and a health agency to work out an alternative after the fact when we now know that there is one available.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: That also can help reduce risks, as we saw no other other.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: people in class and point houses be diagnosed with Legionnaires disease.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Intro 181 is not intended to replace DOHMH's investigation or existing requirements around a building's water system.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: It's just meant to ensure that while those processes are underway, there is also a defined responsibility for getting appropriate information and a practical precaution to people living there.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: I'm interested in hearing from DOHMH today about how Intro 181 can be incorporated into its existing notification and investigation process and how the department would operationalize the 24-hour requirement.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: And truthfully, I'm looking forward to the existing feedback we receive on all the bills before the committee today.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: After carrying this legislation for several years, I hope this hearing positions us to move toward enactment and effective implementation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Thank you again to Chair Shulman for bringing in TRO 181 before the committee, and thank you to my colleagues who have joined me as sponsors of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing back from the administration after today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Amanda Farías
utterances.text: Thank you again.

chapters.summary: Council Member Harvey Epstein discusses his bill to establish temporary Legionnaires testing sites and a digital map, citing confusion among Haven Plaza constituents about where and how to get tested during an outbreak.
chapters.title: Council Member Epstein on Intro 999: testing sites and digital map

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And now we'll go to Councilmember Epstein for a brief statement on his introduction.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman, and thank you, Speaker Menon, for hosting this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: This is a really important conversation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: As the Speaker mentioned earlier, my district, Haven Plaza, is found to have a Legionella bacteria outbreak in their water supply.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: And tenants for months were confused, misinformation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: Information was submitted in writing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: Oral information was contradictory.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: It really is a core function of city government to protect New Yorkers and from public health threats just as Legionnaires here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: Today is a real opportunity for us to learn about what we can do better as the city faces challenges like this one.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: We know this is not the first time, and unfortunately this is not the last time, where we'll see the loss of life.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: As the Speaker mentioned earlier, the loss of 11 people in her and Councilmember Maloney's district is such a tragedy that we as New Yorkers shouldn't have to face again.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: My bill 999 addresses the challenge my constituents face around having access to testing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: When learning about the outbreak, many wanted to get tested.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: However, they were given fragmented and misinformation and confusing information about whether they were qualified for testing or where they could get tested.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: The bill package across the board really establishes a procedure and process to ensure that the Department of Health ensures that hoses can be provided, testing can be provided, information can be provided.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: This is particularly important for adults with compromised immune systems, people with disabilities, and people who had to struggle long distances to get information.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: Getting information is really important for people.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: Getting information about testing sites and Legionnaires is critical.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: It is important for the council to hear directly from the administration how we can improve on what happened this year.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: So when New Yorkers get exposed to Legionnaires in the future, they'll have the resources they need to be able to fight back.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration about

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: what we can do better to affect the lives of impacted New Yorkers, to make sure there are hoses and testing and information, and making sure those cooling towers get tested on a regular basis to improve the lives of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: I want to thank the chair and the speaker again.

utterances.speaker: Harvey Epstein
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing about all the packages of the bills and looking forward to the passage of these important bills.

chapters.summary: Council Member Virginia Maloney introduces her two bills: Intro 1006 requiring cooling tower cleaning three times per year including summer, and Intro 1005 requiring DOHMH public education and outreach about Legionnaires' disease for at-risk populations.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney on Intros 1005 and 1006: cleaning and education

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Now we're going to go to Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: As one of the council members representing the Upper East Side where this outbreak occurred, this is a personal issue to me and to my district.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It's imperative that we get into the details of how this happened and how we can be better prepared as a city to get ahead of a recurring public health emergency that will happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm introducing two bills before the committee today that focus on an improved response time next time.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Intro 1006 strengthens prevention at the source by requiring cooling towers to be cleaned and disinfected at least three times a year,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: including during the summer cooling season when we know we are at highest risk of Legionella bacteria growing.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Intro 1005 focuses on public education and awareness by requiring the Department of Health to conduct outreach on Legionnaire's disease, particularly for New Yorkers who are at higher risk.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: so that people understand the symptoms, their risks, actions to take, and when to seek medical care.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Preventing future outbreaks is going to require a multifaceted approach, stronger prevention, enforcement, better public information, and increased transparency.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're going to, there are a lot of statements from members on their legislation, so what we're going to do is we're going to go to the pre-panel first, so that, because these are people

chapters.summary: Ida Goldstein, married 50 years, describes her husband Robert's two-week hospitalization on life support before dying from Legionnaires contracted through their home window. She calls the death preventable through proper cooling tower cleaning.
chapters.title: Ida Goldstein testifies about husband Robert's death from Legionnaires

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: who are members of the community and victims of Legionella and have, and are family members of victims, so we don't want to keep them here too long.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We have, the first one we have is virtual Ida Goldstein.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: My name is Ida Goldstein.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Now, I'll tell you, Robert was an Air Force veteran and a successful businessman, and he graduated with a Juris Doctorate degree from New York Law School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: I was by his side every day in the hospital, walking back and forth every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Legionnaire came into my home window.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: I am concerned for my safety and anyone else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Bottom line, it could have been avoided easily by having the water towers cleaned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He caught an pneumonia and had a high fever of 104.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Robert was exposed to this poison.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Being in the hospital for over two weeks, he kept declining.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He was on life support and oxygen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: His lungs weren't working well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: His kidneys shut down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He was on antibiotics and brain imaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: His white blood cells increased.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He was going in and out of consciousness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: I was waiting every day to see if he would improve, but he kept getting worse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He was getting thinner every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: My heart was breaking watching him suffer with all this life support attached to his body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: This water vapor that he breathed in with no warning came in our own home from the outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: It took his life away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: And from coming into our privacy of our own home, it murdered him and destroyed me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: We are married 50 years and my loss of him is tremendous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He really fought for his life in every possible way because he said to me, I don't want to leave you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: I am lost without you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: He was my everything, my soulmate, the love of my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: There will never be another one like him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: I was privileged to have him in my life, a true love story, and I don't have him anymore.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are you done or do you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Yes, I'm done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: I'm hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm so sorry for your loss.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ida Goldstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Daniel Thomas describes his 92-year-old father's six-week fight with Legionnaires, including multiple complications and procedures. He calls for stronger enforcement and penalties, noting his father called the disease a 'completely preventable random act of violence.'
chapters.title: Daniel Thomas testifies about father Judge Charles Thomas's death

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We now have Daniel Thomas.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And I appreciate both Speaker Madden and Councilman Shulman's comments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: They're reassuring to hear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: My father was Honorable Judge Charles Thomas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He was born in the Bronx, raised a family in Rockaway Beach, Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And he retired to Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Sure, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Am I still on?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You're mute.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We unmute it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm still on or not.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're having a technical issue we're trying to resolve.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I'm still on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I can't hear myself, but I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Daniel, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: To the extent that my father was a lifelong New Yorker, and he retired in 2010 from the Queens County Supreme Court bench, and he resided in Manhattan on the Upper East Side until the time he passed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: My father was actually a very, very pragmatic person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He understood that not everything can be fixed, not everything can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: But when he received the notice that he had Legionella, July 2nd, I took him to the hospital, and he fought valiantly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: To the surprise of many of the doctors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He survived six weeks fighting this disease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He encountered numerous complications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He had two life-saving procedures to fix arterial bleeds that developed in the stress ulcers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: His body filled up with fluid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He looked like the Pillsbury Doughboy, based on the amount of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: fluid his body was holding because it was fighting this Legionella that is so toxic, it completely alters and creates a cascade effect to any existing problems that you may have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: But he was independent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He walked the neighborhood on the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He went to the bank, went shopping, went to the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He was a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: A member of society that was still contributing, still working, still helping young lawyers, counseling them, guiding them, giving advices to other judges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And the amount of pain that he went through enduring this disease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He knew.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He was compos mentis the whole time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He never lost any of his faculties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He was aware.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He made goodbye videos to his grandkids and his children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: When they approached him, said, you may need this procedure that is not going to, you're not going to survive this procedure that you need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: But he did, and he was strong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: But he wasn't strong enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And the thing that the public needs to know and this committee needs to know, the reason Legionella is so deadly to the elderly is because it creates a cascade effect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And you don't have the strength to weather the storm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: There's not enough runway of health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: That can make you last.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: The doctor said normal ammonia, you can get over in a matter of weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Legionella is going to be months, and the body weakens on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And it was very, very difficult for myself and my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Watch my father deteriorate to the point where

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: He knew.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And what he said to me was, this was a completely preventable random act of violence that occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And my whole life I've been about justice, doling it out, making sure it was done properly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And this was unjust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: So enforcement absolutely has to be stepped up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And I appreciate that the city is making changes, but they're not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: They're not enough because they were not effective enough to prevent this outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: The 2025 outbreak in Harlem should have been a wake-up call to the entire city, every building owner, everyone who's doing enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: We cannot scrimp.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: We cannot cut corners on safety when it's completely preventable, completely avoidable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And my father in the hospital said to me, what kind of judge, what kind of jurist would I be if I didn't stand up for myself and my own rights?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And he researched a very, very fine attorney, Ron Catter, and said, I want Ron Catter to represent me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I will not live to see the end of this matter, but I do want to see change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I want my grandkids to know that my death was not in vain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And to the extent that enforcement is also part of what the penalty is, I don't know that the penalties are strong enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I would ask this committee to consider what penalties there are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: We have tremendous means and technology today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Whether it's shutting down a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: electrical systems for these air cooling, for these cooling towers, or the buildings themselves, to force compliance if necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: It's great that there's all these, you know, millions of dollars that are in arrears from buildings that haven't complied, but that does no good for the New Yorkers walking the streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: So there's much more I could say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I'm happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: At a later date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: But for right now, I want to share with you that the enforcement is key.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: I'm delighted to hear that no death is acceptable from Legionella in this city at this time that we live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: No death is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And to put it in context, I read an article about a fighter jet that the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: Military has that cost $150 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: And there's an ejection seat in that fighter jet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: That tells you how precious life is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Thomas
utterances.text: So the fact that my father was 92 doesn't change the fact that he had still life ahead of him, and he was robbed, and his life was taken away.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Daniel, I just want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I know it's obviously very painful to have to come and to talk about the loss of your father.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We very much appreciate you doing that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I want to extend condolences to you, to your family, and condolences to Ida, who spoke earlier.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Ida and I had a conversation right after her husband died.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: She told me,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: with much love about her 50-year marriage to her husband, and I know it's very painful, Ida, for you to have to talk about this, but we appreciate you doing so as well, and our deepest condolences.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thomas.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Condolences as well.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And we appreciate you testifying because it makes a difference for us.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Minister Sandra Coleman, president of One Night to Advocates and Isaac Houses resident, calls Legionnaires 100% preventable and criticizes the health department for not hiring adequate inspectors. She reports seniors hospitalized with kidney failure from the disease.
chapters.title: Sandra Coleman testifies on Legionnaires impact at Isaac Houses

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Now we're going to go, we have an in-person panel.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We have Minister...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Sandra Coleman.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Just come and take a seat.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And Valerie Mason.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Minister, you can go first.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: Greetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: Greetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: My name is Sandra I.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: Coleman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: I am a minister, the president of One Night to Advocates, and the co-founder of the Home Sizes Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: I reside at Isaac Houses on the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: Legionnaires disease is 100% preventable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: We should not be here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: Have we not learned from the seven souls lost in Harlem last year?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: One death is too many.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra I. Coleman
utterances.text: I repeat, one death is too many.

utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Lastly, pre-insure 2422 would require us to maintain a public database of locations impacted by Legionella.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: As I outlined in the five new measures put forward by the Mamdani administration, the health department will provide a map to supplement our existing address-based online lookup tool for cooling tower inspections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That tool allows any New Yorker to enter an address and see the registered towers at or near it, with each tower's registration status, inspection history, and the Legionella sampling compliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Mason
utterances.text: We were overwhelmed with inquiries about whether people should be able to go to the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The map will show the cooling tower locations and the lookup tool provides recent inspection results.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: However, mapping diagnosed cases in building investigations or community clusters of Legionnaire's disease could jeopardize patient confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing all of the legislation further with City Council.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: In conclusion, thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Thank you to the members of the committee for your attention and commitment to this issue.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We look forward to working together to further strengthen our city's Legionnaires disease prevention and response infrastructure.

chapters.summary: Martin concludes by referencing a detailed day-by-day timeline appendix provided to the committee, reiterates the hearing is about honoring those who died, and expresses readiness to answer questions.
chapters.title: Commissioner Martin concludes testimony with appendix timeline reference

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Before I conclude my testimony, I'd like to direct your attention to the appendix and the printed copies you all have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I've walked through the major points in our response to the Upper East Side Legionnaires cluster this July, but this testimony is not a comprehensive report.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: To that end, we have included a

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: timeline detailing every single step of our response day by day.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I hope you'll find it a useful record.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Each step we took to cut off any bacterial source was in service of keeping as many New Yorkers out of harm's way as possible.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I want to end today where I began.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This hearing is ultimately about honoring the people who died in connection with this summer's cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: As we continue to discuss the technical details of our interventions, I want to keep their memory at the heart of this work.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm now going to hand it over to Speaker Menon for her round of questioning.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin asks why source identification is taking longer than in previous outbreaks (35 days in Harlem, 26 in Bronx). Dr. Howard explains over 300 isolates are undergoing whole genome sequencing from 59 culture-positive towers and patient samples, expected this fall.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions Commissioner on source identification delays

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner, and to your team for being here today and for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I know I have a lot of questions, and I'm sure my colleagues do as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'll begin with some of them, and I'll probably then come back on a second round as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I really wanted to start off with asking if you've determined the source of the 2026 cluster.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I obviously saw what you said in your testimony, but have you been able to winnow it down from a source for a residential building, a commercial building, or a city-owned building?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, first of all, thank you again, Speaker Menon, and thank you, Chair Shulman, for bringing us here today.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Before I talk about where we are with the source, let me just say a few words about the 11 New Yorkers who have passed.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Each one of those deaths is a tragedy, and our hearts are with the loved ones, with the friends, with the families.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And each New Yorker who lost their life, their life,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: in this process requires us to examine every single thing that we can about this response and to identify ways to push our nation-leading Legionella laws even further.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Now, to answer your question directly, the process of identifying the exact match, pinpointing the cooling tower or tower, is it responsible, is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We're doing something called whole genome sequencing right now.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: My hope is that we're going to be able to provide a match, that there will be one or two, as there were last year, matches.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But we don't have that data back yet.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We should be able to report on that later this summer, or later this fall.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I guess my response to that is why is it taking so long?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because in the Harlem outbreak, the department released the results of the source within 35 days or so.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In the Bronx outbreak, they released their results, and I believe it was 26 days.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So it's now been two months.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This is a very complicated process where we're looking to make the match between the DNA that we take from the bacteria in the patient's samples and to match them to the DNA that's in the bacteria in the associated cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so this process is complicated, it's complex, and it takes time.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me pass it to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Howard to share a little bit more about the process and where we are.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So as you heard earlier, that there were over 180 cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: We had 59 cooling tower samples that were culture positive.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And for each of these cultures, we may have multiple isolates that undergo whole genome sequencing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: We actually do two different culture methods.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And for each culture, there can be...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: More than one isolates.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: One of those cultures is a solid culture that's done on a petri dish.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And depending upon the sample, we can have five colonies of bacteria that grow, or we could have 20.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And there can be more than one species of Legionella that grow on the petri dish from that one

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: cooling tower sample.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And so the technicians will sample isolates from multiple colonies on the petri dish.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So they are doing whole genome sequencing on over 300 isolates.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: That includes isolates both from the cooling tower samples as well as from a handful of patients.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And that takes time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: After we have the whole genome sequencing is the analysis to look for that potential genetic match, an identical fingerprint between patient samples and environmental samples.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So when will we expect then precisely to have the...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These results?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: We expect that later this fall.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Menin questions why inspections dropped from 5,000 in 2017 to 1,100 by mid-2025. Commissioner Martin says inspections are up 30% year-over-year and are one layer of a multi-layered system. Deputy Commissioner Schiff notes staffing shortages and ongoing recruitment.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin presses on declining inspection numbers

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to move on to inspections.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: According to reports,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I know Chair Shulman referenced this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Inspectors inspected more than 5,000 towers in 2017.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: By mid-2025, the number had fallen to just over 1,100.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Why are we inspecting so few towers compared to nine years ago?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So our inspection work is really the sort of third layer of defense that we have when we think about the

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: system that exists to protect the city from Legionnaires disease clusters.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The first layer is really what the owners need to be doing on a daily, weekly, and monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The second layer from our standpoint is to ask

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And because of the law that was implemented from last year's 2025 Legionella law,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: they also now need to submit this monthly Legionella sampling to allow us to investigate how they are doing, how owners are doing with the daily, the weekly, and the consistent actions that need to be taken.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The third layer of defense in this system is what you've described, is us doing these inspections, going actually physically to these cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And the fourth layer is if we find things that are wrong, if there's things that need to be immediately addressed or adjusted, we...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: enforce and issue summonses which turn into fines and we order corrective action to be taken.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: All of these layers together are coming together to help to reduce the risk of Legionnaires disease clusters and one of the layers that we have as I mentioned here is inspections.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me talk about the rates of inspections.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Our inspections this time last year compared to last are up 30%, over 30%.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And that work is critical, but it is also not the only layer.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to interrupt you because it's not about what's happening right now after the outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's what didn't happen before the outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because obviously we know now the department is doing far more inspections after the outbreak has already occurred.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
