utterances.text: What I'm concerned about is, according to reports, the department issued no violations in the three zip codes covering the Upper East Side in January, March, May, and June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The department issued 20 summons to six buildings in February, five summons to one building in April.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me answer that question, but let me come back to clarify the previous.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The 30% increase number, Madam Speaker, is not after the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That level of inspections was higher even before the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So the new water ecologist positions, the funding that we got, that has made a difference.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And more inspections have happened even now.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: before this cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me pass it to Deputy Commissioner Corinne Schiff to talk about the monthly summonses and inspections you just asked about.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Speaker, we're still looking at the data that was in the council report to see if our data matches that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But I would say a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: First, as we have discussed last year, we were short-staffed, and that's why we were not meeting our goals to inspect every cooling tower annually.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And as the commissioner testified, we were authorized to hire additional staff in November 2025, and we have been actively recruiting.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that is why our inspections are up about 35% citywide since the start of this year.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And as we continue to bring staff on and train them, those inspection rates will go up.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: As the Commissioner said, inspections are one part of our overall program to promote compliance among cooling tower

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: operators with the Council's nation-leading, incredibly protective laws and the regulations that we have issued to detail for owners how to comply with those local law mandates.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So in addition to inspections, which are an important part of promoting compliance, we also offer guidance that we publish on our website and we make available to owners.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have individual consultations.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We send out reminders at key points of the year.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have newsletters that we publish on key topics.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We hold training sessions.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: All of these are designed to support owners who have very specific requirements that they have to implement all the time.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There's work for them to do many times a week, weekly, monthly.

chapters.summary: Menin highlights zero violations in the cluster zip codes in January, March, May, and June, then 180 in July. She questions why there wasn't more proactive enforcement heading into summer. Martin and Schiff defend the multi-layered compliance approach.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin confronts lack of pre-outbreak violations in cluster area

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, but it doesn't, I guess I have a very specific question, which is,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It appears from the data that the department didn't issue any violations in this affected cluster area in January, March, May, and June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: As I mentioned, 20 summons to six buildings in February, five summons to one building in April, and then suddenly in July, 180 summons to 78 buildings.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So look, we obviously want to see the increased enforcement, but what we're trying to get to here is why there wasn't enforcement when we knew the summer months were coming, and then why is there no data about the number of inspections?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: From 2026.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Normally that data is made public in June and July.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We, our team is telling us we cannot access any data.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So if that has changed, we would want to know that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But as of when the committee report was written, our team was telling us there was no data made public about the number of inspections from 2026.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me share just a few words and then we'll see if Deputy Commissioner has anything else to add.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, we have been consistently issuing summonses, violations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This last year, in 2025, this amounted to over 1,300.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: violations in total totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars six hundred eighty thousand dollars in fines within the cluster region that you you described

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: we also issued summonses and violations over 110 as part of this cluster 15 of those were public health hazards 50 were critical violations 40 were general violations

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: so the enforcement apparatus right we have two jobs as part of what we do in our regulatory system.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The first is to reduce the risk of Legionnaires disease clusters.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The second is when they happen to respond aggressively, transparently, and quickly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And the violations that you see here are us doing that part of helping to reduce the risk.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Right, but those violations occurred.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: After the outbreak had occurred.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's really our point.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our point that we're trying to make is we want to understand why when Legionella bacteria is no surprise and

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: happening in the summer months, which is why the council originally passed Council Member Shulman's law over a year ago that went into effect on May 8th, why there was not more violations.

chapters.summary: Menin presses why 21 of 56 authorized water ecologist positions were unfilled heading into summer. Martin clarifies 50 of 56 are now filled with 6 open, and says the majority were filled before the cluster. Menin disputes this based on her data.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin on water ecologist vacancies before outbreak

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In addition, during the outbreak, only 35 of 56 authorized water ecologist positions were staffed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Heading into the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So there were 21 authorized positions that the department never staffed with active inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: on that speaker.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There are 56 total budgeted positions for the water ecologists.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: 50 of those positions either have people who are on the ground, on the roofs, I was with some of them just a couple weeks ago doing our water inspections, or going through the onboarding process.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There are folks who we have not recruited, we have not hired.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We have six open positions, and we are trying to make sure we get the right people for each of those roles.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Those are highly specialized roles.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But the vast majority of these, even the new positions that we got, were filled and had folks either on the ground or on board.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Right, but not before the outbreak occurred.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The point is that...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Why between January and May, heading into the summer months, did the department leave 21 authorized positions of active inspectors open?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's the point.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Very good that now it's being filled, but our point is that had the department have filled these vacant positions, we would probably not be in this situation that we're in right now.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So that's what I'm trying to get to.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If we could move on.

chapters.summary: Menin asks why few violations were issued in May and June if 25% of buildings were non-compliant with the new law. Martin says compliance was 74% in the cluster region and 77% citywide, and transparency measures pushed it to 97%.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin on 25% non-compliance and lack of pre-summer enforcement

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How many buildings were non-compliant with Chair Shulman's 2025 law when it went into effect in May and June?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our understanding of the data, please correct us if we're incorrect, is that 25% of buildings were not in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So why were there so few violations issued in May and June if there were 25% non-compliant buildings?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Across the city, citywide compliance with the new law was 77%.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That was about eight weeks after the new law had gone into effect.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Within the region, within the cluster region, compliance was 74%.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: While the cluster carried on, as you know, we decided to take the most transparent step we've ever done as part of these clusters, and we released the names of the PCR-positive buildings.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And by the end of this cluster, through that process, 97% of those towers that we inspected were compliant.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And that's why the lesson that we learned from this process is that this transparency is a critical feature, critical part of the work to increase compliance on this brand new law.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And that's why one of our measures that we announced just yesterday is to further increase the transparency by

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: allowing residents to use this new tool where they can put their address in and get a map to see what the compliance history is of the towers in their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that's, I guess, and I'm sure Chair Shulman will talk about that, but that is why we wanted, coming into the summer months, the proactive enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Again, this is sort of one of the themes that's coming out in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We need far more proactive enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: If there were 25% noncompliant buildings, there should have been far more active enforcement heading into the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I have many more questions, but then I'm going to go.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I pass it on to Chair Shulman.

chapters.summary: Menin cites an NBC report that DOHMH has no alert system to trigger enforcement when owners miss reporting deadlines. Schiff explains the follow-up program for positive results but does not directly address automated flagging of missed deadlines.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions lack of automated alert system for non-compliance

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It was publicly reported by Melissa Rousseau of NBC that the department currently has no alert system to trigger quick enforcement when a building owner fails to comply with the new cooling tower rules, including the requirement under

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Chair Shulman's bill to report Legionella testing every 31 days.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And if so, why doesn't the city's portal automatically or through some type of manual follow-up flag miss five-day reporting deadlines or overdue 31-day testing requirements for immediate review and enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We do have a process by capturing whether or not someone is compliant with that 31-day sampling requirement.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it to Deputy Commissioner Karanja for more.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The local law requires reporting the level, the highest level

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: of Legionella bacteria to the department, which is when we get to the point where we really want to be providing ongoing assistance to that cooling tower operator.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it is in the local law and also in our regulation that when Legionella bacteria, when the results from that sample and the council's innovation to increase the

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: frequency of sampling to monthly is giving owners much more information.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: When they get that result back that shows that they have a level of bacteria where it's

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: starting to show that they're no longer adequately controlling the bacteria growth in that cooling tower.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They report that information to us, and we have a follow-up program to make sure that they are conducting the appropriate corrective action for that, that they are taking their compliance samples, that those compliance samples are showing that that remediation was

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: effective, and if not, that they are continuing to remediate.

chapters.summary: Menin questions why DOHMH declared the cluster exposure ended on July 31 when four more deaths were reported afterward. Martin explains the exposure had ended based on the two-week incubation period, and Dr. Howard explains delayed death reporting from prolonged hospitalizations.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions July 31 'mission accomplished' press release

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, one more question I'm going to ask before passing it to Sarah Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So on July 31st, the department issued a press release.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New York City Health Department declares Upper East Side Legionnaires disease cluster exposure has ended.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: However, after that time, four more deaths were reported.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I guess, why did the department feel it was necessary to put that press release out?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, obviously we agree and we don't contest that the exposure ended on that date, but to take sort of that mission accomplished when people were still, many people were still in the hospital and then four deaths were reported subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me sort of divide this into two separate segments.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So the first is the exposure had ended, and we typically use a clock of two weeks after the last person who developed symptoms was found to have developed those symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So that was two weeks into the period that we were at, which was July 31st.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: From the perspective of

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: of the risk to New Yorkers, we wanted to make sure that we updated New Yorkers to know that the risk had been eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Now, the second question that you're asking is around the continuing case count.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So I'm going to turn it over to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Howard to talk a little bit more about how that process works.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And I just first want to acknowledge that every death is a tragedy, and I offer my condolences to the family members of those who passed.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So even though we knew the source was eliminated, that doesn't mean our work doesn't continue.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And Legionnaire's disease is one of the diseases that is reportable to the New York City Health Department.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And for every report that comes in, the epidemiologists have to do a case investigation.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: First, they review medical records to confirm that it meets the case definition, and then do an interview of the patient or a family member to determine a potential source of exposure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Now, even though the source was eliminated, that process was still continuing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: The reason why we identified additional deaths after the source had been eliminated, there's a few possible explanations.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: In some instances, an individual may have been exposed in the area, but may have traveled out of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And we might not have known about that death until some time later.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: In other instances, it can be difficult to reach a family member at this difficult time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So there are delays in getting the information that we need in order to confirm that an individual was exposed to the area.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And third, some people who are diagnosed weeks ago succumb to that illness after a prolonged hospitalization.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So that's why we can have additional deaths, even though the source of exposure has been eliminated.

chapters.summary: Schulman raises that the Legionnaires dashboard was closed after the July 31 press release and couldn't be updated with four subsequent deaths. Martin says this follows the same approach used in previous clusters, and the website has since been updated with all 11 deaths.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin and Chair Schulman on dashboard not updating post-declaration

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: agencies, legionnaires, dashboards.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: literally say you cannot report any additional data.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So once the department issued that press release, if you go to that dashboard, you cannot update it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So even though four additional people passed away since that press release, none of that information could be uploaded onto the dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It just says the dashboard is

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: sort of closed for business, like you can't edit it.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And that's what we've done in previous clusters, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We have a period of time that we do our investigation, our cluster, and when the exposure is over, we don't continue to update the public dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This was not something that was new in this cluster.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But for those family members that their loved one passed away, I mean, there are four people who lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And it just seems to me that it would be common sense that the dashboard, as additional people tragically lose their lives or additional people are perhaps hospitalized, that the health department would

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: acknowledge that and update the dashboard accordingly so that the public writ large can get accurate information.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Every single one of those lives lost is a tragedy for us, and we have acknowledged those lives.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There were many, many public communications in which we did so, including in this testimony.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The dashboard itself is one specific measure that we use.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But according to our typical approach, we did what we've done in the past.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: with regard to the publication of the dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to pass it over to Chair Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about Legionella entry, growth conditions, and water temperature ranges. Schiff provides the range of 68-113 degrees Fahrenheit and explains about half of cooling towers operate year-round, with inspections planned accordingly.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman questions how Legionella enters and grows in cooling towers

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have a lot of questions, so I'm going to ask a number of them, and then I'm going to do, as the speaker did, let my colleagues ask, and then we'll go to a second round.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How does Legionella first enter a cooling tower or water system?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are there ways to prevent the initial growth?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Legionella bacteria is found ubiquitously.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It's common in the environment, and it can basically contaminate warm, stagnant water, which is found in cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: With what water temperatures are most conducive to Legionella growth?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I presume there's a certain turning point there.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When is the water in a cooling tower most likely to reach those temperatures?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So those are two separate questions.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It is warm, stagnant water that is the most...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Suitable type of environment for the...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, does it...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Like, is it at 85 degrees, then that's more likely, or is it...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, or it just...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It doesn't...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, I'm just trying to...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, we can get back to you on the exact temperatures, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That would be...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And when is the water in the cooling tower most likely to reach that temperature as it's sitting there?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because it takes a while, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It may not be the first day of when it's hot.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It may be the second day.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me pass it over to Deputy Commissioner Branshaw.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We can get you the temperature ranges, but I think what's important is that the council has recognized that the cooling tower is an ideal environment for the growth of Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that is why you have set out such detailed requirements for the owners to constantly monitor and maintain those.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And in our regulations, we set out further details.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And this is so important because the owners have to maintain these cooling towers literally every single day.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They can't let their guard down.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: For the very reasons that you say, Chair, the cooling tower holds a tub of warm water.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that is why they are constantly treating it.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And really the system has, you could say, belts and suspenders.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They're doing visual inspections.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They're adding biocide all the time.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They have a protocol that they have to develop for their specific tower, their specific cooling tower system, and how it operates at their specific building.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Because we know that there is so much risk.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that is why there is such detailed oversight required by the owners.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No, and I appreciate that, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I just, you know, for educational purposes, I think it would just be good for us to kind of know this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying exactly, but I think it helps with the process of just the layperson, too.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, just to get a sense.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Like, it's not, when it's 30 degrees out, you're not going to have Legionella, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So what we know is that typically when we have these clusters, they're happening during the summer or the late spring.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so, yes, absolutely, the warmer the water is, the more likely it is to harbor.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And it's when they actually, now let me ask a question.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: My understanding, I may be wrong, is that the cooling towers don't function unless, because they function to cool the building off, right?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So it wouldn't function necessarily in the winter.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is that sort of, so it's when they actually are.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it to Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: About half of the cooling tower systems in the city operate.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: year-round and about half are seasonal.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I can give you the temperature, 68 to 113 degrees Fahrenheit is the range.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And you're right also to say that as our climate is warming, we see additional risk.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so that is why we were so supportive of your bill last year to increase the sampling to monthly because it gives owners in that whole monitoring and maintenance program, gives them more information every month.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They're getting more information as a check.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: How is their constant ongoing monitoring and maintenance program?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: How is it going?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They're getting more information about that and able to make adjustments to their program.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: To your point about some of them operate year-round and some don't, you have, I assume there's a list of them, right, of which ones operate year-round and which don't.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The ones that operate year-round, do they get more, do you, are you more,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: involved in making sure that they are complying that the ones that don't operate year-round when they're not operating they're not operating right so

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: but are you more vigilant about the ones that operate year-round so we we are vigilant about all of them right and I didn't mean to but we but so the one so we this is how we plan our inspections so we want to we want to inspect when they are operating right

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: and so we are that's that's how we plan our year so the ones that are operating all year we can we can do those inspections.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: in the cooler months and the ones that are operating only in the warmer months, we focus the inspections at that time.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how bacteria spreads from cooling towers to people. Martin explains contaminated mist expelled from towers can carry bacteria that people inhale, and wind can spread it across neighborhoods, which is why a broad geographic area is investigated.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on how Legionnaires spreads from towers to infection

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask that you, by the way, we've been joined by Councilmember Areola, I just want to acknowledge.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you walk us through how exactly, because I would like to know, I think others would too, how Legionnaire's disease spreads from the

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: initial proliferation of Legionella bacteria in a cooling tower or building water system through the release of contaminated water droplets to the development of infection?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This is an educational, yes.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, so what we see with Legionnaire's disease clusters like the one that we're talking about here today is the Legionella bacteria contaminates that water, that warm, stagnant water we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And then that water, the mist.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That is expelled from the top of the cooling tower, that mist can carry

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: small amounts of that bacteria and people inhale that mist and then that is what can basically trigger the beginning of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do we know, like how long does it take to get to a point where

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do we know that?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Where, get point, to which point?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When it gets to the point of like becoming, you know, a deadly bacteria that, I mean, how long does it have to, what, fester in the water?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is it, as soon as it becomes?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As soon as it's detected, that's at the point.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You mean the valve?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: of bacteria in the cooling tower.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's such an important question and it's one that we don't really know.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that's part of, that is one of the challenges.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so that is why the regulation sets out tiers for response because we want,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: and again, why the monthly sampling is so important, although we are in early days, so we don't know yet how effective that's going to be, but our idea is it's going to give operators very early information when that bacteria is starting to grow so they can take corrective action,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: do their confirmatory sampling and see if it's happened and see if that remediation has been effective.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And if not, then there's the next step for them to do to continue to remediate.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So there isn't a perfect answer to your very important question.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No, and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And so.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Doctor, from what you said, so if it's really windy out and you have it, it can spread further, I'm guessing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Well, you're putting your finger on something that's very important, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So when we have these clusters,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It is not clear where exactly the source is, and the mist that comes from the coin tower can absolutely migrate.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And that's why we have a fairly large region that we look at.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: In this case, it was these three zip codes that we were looking at because of exactly what you're describing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You expanded, I think, the zip code, too, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We did, actually, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And maybe I can...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Pass it to Corinne Schifter to describe a little bit more on that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I would say that when these clusters happen, we're really doing detective work in different parts of the department.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We're getting information from my team that's taking samples from the cooling towers and knows where the cooling towers are, from Dr.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Howard's team who's doing case investigations, and from the laboratory scientists who are telling us what's happening from the cooling tower samples.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And as more information comes in, that helps us further define the area of risk.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so sometimes, as we did here, the initial area, we needed to expand it.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And really, the thing that we are trying to do is get that message out to New Yorkers, because we know that once the cases have started, that exposure is underway, and we want to get that message to people.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They've already been exposed.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We want them to listen to their bodies and get quickly into health care.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how first symptomatic patients are identified and whether providers can be generally alerted to test for Legionnaires. Martin describes syndromic surveillance from ERs and notes a joint health advisory with NYS was sent to all physicians on June 1st before the cluster.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on early patient identification and provider awareness

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How are the first symptomatic patients identified at the beginning of an outbreak or cluster?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What kinds of testing and care infrastructure are required to ensure that infected individuals are identified and receive care as quickly as possible and to ensure that DOHMH's outbreak response can be activated in a timely manner?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, let me first start by saying that we have an incredible team of epidemiologists at the health department that are doing the work every single day to identify these cases.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And they work in conjunction with data that's coming in from our many tools.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: that can basically help to identify their patterns.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So it's both sort of intuition from the epidemiologists as well as them reviewing the information that's coming in from things like syndromic surveillance, which you know is

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: a tool that we have that allows us to ingest the information from all the ERs in the city.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that once you identify somebody, then you talk to all the providers in the area and, you know, et cetera, and all of that to be aware.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But is it possible to just make providers aware in general that if somebody comes in with flu-like symptoms, you know, they get tested right away for COVID, they get tested right away for the flu, if there's a way for them to be tested for Legionnaires?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And that's exactly what we did this time.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So before this cluster began on June 1st, we did what's known as a health advisory out to all physicians in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We jointly did that with New York State to alert providers, facilities, and clinical laboratories that, you know, summer months are here.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Make sure to put this on your differential.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I'm an ER physician, and getting that kind of advisory for me would make this top of mind for me going into my ER shift.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so that's why we do these health advisories.

chapters.summary: Schulman points out a press release lists first cases as June 27 and 29, while the Legionnaires webpage shows June 23. Martin explains the difference between symptom onset dates and diagnosis dates, and agrees to look into the specific discrepancy.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman flags discrepancy in first case dates on DOHMH websites

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, I wanted to just bring to your attention, so there's a press release on

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Your site on the DOHMH site that says the first cases happened in as of 627 and 629.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But if you go to the DOHMH Legionnaires webpage, it shows the first case was on 623.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So what's the discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Can you share more about which sites you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So is it, what site are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: DOHMH did a press release.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So it's on the DOHMH site.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: There's a press release about the second death in Upper East Side Legionnaires disease.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And then it lists in that press release, it lists the first cases as from 627 and 629.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But if you go to your Legionnaires webpage, it shows the first case was all the way back on 623.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I'm just asking what the discrepancy is.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I don't know if it's an error or whatever, but because people are...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Going up and looking at that stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I just want to point that out.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd have to look at the exact sites that you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You can take a look and then circle back with us.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I would, yeah, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me share, there are two different clocks that we look at when it comes to Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There's the symptom onset date, and then there's the diagnosis date.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So someone might be diagnosed, for instance, on July 5th, but their symptoms might start July 1st.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because if the first case was on 6-23, that's a big difference from it being a week later.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, we...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We can look into it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So just, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So take a look and see if you can get back to us.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks whether someone must enter a building to be exposed and whether Legionella can spread between cooling towers. Martin says the entire geographic area is at risk from mist, and Schiff says they don't know if bacteria spreads between towers.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on who is at risk and whether bacteria spreads between towers

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When there is Legionella growth in a building's cooling tower, who is at risk of infection?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does someone have to live in the building or physically enter the building to be potentially exposed?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When there's Legionella in a building's cooling tower, who is at risk of infection?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does someone have to live in the building or physically enter the building to be potentially exposed?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You're saying no, but I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, we are concerned when there's a cluster about the whole geography, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Because as we talked about earlier, the microscopic water vapor can have Legionella bacteria in it, and it can spread across the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So that's why we issue broad guidance in those zip codes.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So here's an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can Legionella bacteria spread between cooling towers?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That is an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it to Corrine Shipp to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It is an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have asked it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We don't know.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Interesting.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do all cooling towers that test positive in a specific area contribute to the cluster?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Do all cooling towers in a...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That tests positive.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Contribute to the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In a specific area contribute to the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Okay, this is...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, so this is important.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There's two questions that...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: we're trying to answer when it comes to the sampling and the testing in the region.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The first question we're trying to answer is, is there a genetic match between the Legionella that's part of the sputum that we get from the patient to a specific cooling tower?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That gives us the ability to say this cluster came from this cooling tower.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So that's the first question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That's whole genome sequencing can make that match.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There's a separate question that we're asking in a cluster, and that is which cooling towers have high levels of Legionella bacteria in it.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And those two questions.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Are answering different parts of the operations.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about PCR vs. culture testing, turnaround times, lab capacity, and whether 30 certified labs are sufficient. Martin explains PCR takes 24-48 hours, culture takes two weeks, and there are no current capacity concerns. He also describes patient diagnostic testing including urine antigen tests.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on testing methods, lab capacity, and turnaround times

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How can people protect themselves from potential exposure?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The number one most important way folks can protect themselves when we have these clusters is to understand the signs and symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And to get in to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This is a highly treatable condition, but it does require individuals getting to appropriate care and getting evaluated.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The department conducted over 360 tests and collected samples from more than 180 cooling towers during the Upper East Side outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Where do collected samples go for analysis, and how does DOHMH choose where to send the samples?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So those samples are coming to us, to our public health lab, where we are doing our own testing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: An evaluation of those samples.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In the announcement that was made yesterday about some of the proposals, one of them talked about faster testing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What was that faster testing of?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I wasn't clear on that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So we are always looking to improve our system and identify ways to further strengthen our regulatory apparatus.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Was it testing of the cooling towers or it's testing of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It's testing of the cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So that's one of the things that we want to do is figure out if there are new types of novel testing measures to speed up.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The testing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many laboratories are currently certified and available to analyze cooling tower samples for Legionella in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: At this moment, we don't have concerns about capacity, and we also have our own testing capacity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Those labs, they're standardized testing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In other words, everything is done the same way in each lab?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So the New York State currently does that certification for these labs.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so that's the sort of...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do different labs have different turnaround times for, you know, again, going back to for the lab tests?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we are at the mercy of the bacterial culture process with the testing that we do with rotabacterial culture testing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That takes two weeks here, and it takes two weeks up in Albany.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It's the same, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do these laboratories have sufficient capacity to meet the new monthly testing requirements, particularly during the summer or a community outbreak?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, at this moment we don't have concerns about the capacity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No, okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Please explain the difference between a PCR test and a culture test.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The PCR test is asking the question, is there evidence of Legionella DNA in the sample?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The DNA can't tell us if it's live or dead, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It could be that there was Legionella bacteria at some point.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Culture is asking a different question.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It's asking right now.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Is there live bacteria in the sample?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So these are two separate questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is the turnaround time to receive results from each test, and then are there any other testing methods which may be more efficient or effective?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There are three main tests that we use.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The first is PCR testing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The turnaround time is between 24 to 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Culture testing is the second.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That takes up to two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And then there's whole genome sequencing, which takes a much longer time.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So the PCR testing is done when somebody shows up with symptoms and is...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Ah, the testing that I just mentioned is the testing of the samples of the water and the cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The testing of the individual, there's a number of different tests that we do if somebody has potential Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We do a urine.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: antigen tests, we can do x-rays, we do other blood tests.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so that sort of picture gets put together by doing these different types of testing all together.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So if somebody had, so the initial test when somebody comes in and that's positive, then they would get treatment at that point or it has to wait for other testing?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it over to Deputy Commissioner Andrea Howard.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So as when a patient goes to see a provider,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: the first thing that clinician would do, you know, based upon the signs and symptoms, would evaluate that patient and then make a decision on a differential diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: For Legionnaire's disease, first of all, you have to have pneumonia and you have to have a positive Legionella test.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: A urinary antigen test can take a few days to come back.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: A culture of the sputum could take up to two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: However, as a practicing infectious disease physician, if I had a strong suspicion that someone had Legionnaire's disease, you could start them presumptively on treatment right away.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And in addition, to consider other diagnoses, including other forms of pneumonia.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Schulman questions the $1.5 million contract awarded to New Jersey-based EMSL Analytical, asking why an out-of-state vendor was chosen and what role they play. Schiff clarifies EMSL handles routine samples while the public health lab handles cluster samples, and has a New York branch.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on EMSL Analytical contract and lab testing roles

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is because it's clear that if we get to it early, the patient will do a lot better the earlier that we get to it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Absolutely, and that's why our most urgent message to the public is to monitor for symptoms and to present to a clinician promptly if they have symptoms suggestive of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Don't wait, don't try to think it's allergies, don't try to self-treat, but see a provider who can provide that medical care.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Earlier this year, DOHMH announced its intention to award EMSL Analytical Inc., a New Jersey-based environmental testing firm, a $1.5 million contract for Legionella environmental testing, including PCR and culture testing,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: through July 31, 2032.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: DOHMH awarded this contract to EMSL on August 21.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does the public health laboratory conduct any Legionella environmental testing?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You said they did.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I'm going to hand it to Corinne Shea from that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: The lab does do our testing, and as we just testified, during a cluster, we will send the cooling tower samples to the lab.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: For our routine work, when we take samples, we send them to a commercial lab.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Why was an out-of-state vendor chosen for this contract?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are there any New York City or New York State-based firms that could have fulfilled these responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: We went through the procurement process.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What role will ESM-L play in the testing process?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Will they be responsible for collecting samples?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Will they test the samples in their own labs?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Or will they outsource to other labs?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: This is the lab that we will use for our routine samples.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, so you've used it before.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't know that we've used them before.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have an agreement with a contract with a commercial lab for our routine samples.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: For our cluster samples, we send to our own lab.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So the procurement process, if you can, I mean, I know you don't have that on hand, but if we can know what the procurement process was to select the lab, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are turnaround times on testing results guaranteed as part of your contract with the MSL?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you say that again?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Turnaround times on testing results guaranteed as part of your contract.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do have provisions about turnaround times, and I will also add that EMSL does have a New York branch.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about the Department of Buildings' role during outbreaks. Martin describes learning from the 2025 unregistered cooling tower discovery and working with DOB over 5-6 months to formalize cross-referencing of registration data, now announced as a new measure.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on DOB coordination during outbreaks

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is the Department of Buildings'role during an outbreak, and how does DOHMH coordinate with DOB to ensure buildings are complying with orders and requirements?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So as you know from last year, Chair, we found an unregistered cooling tower that at the time was operated by a private company that was at the source of that cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, we learned from that experience, we understood that identifying these unregistered cooling towers is a priority, and we put that into practice immediately.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We've been working with Department of Buildings over the course of the last five to six months to really build out this process, and we're happy to

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: point to this new measure that we announced yesterday, which will formalize that and make it automatic, the fact that our systems talk to each other and allow us to share that information back and forth to potentially catch unregistered cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to, I have a lot more questions, but I'm going to let my colleagues ask and come back around.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether violations found during the outbreak response could have been identified earlier through routine inspections. Schiff explains inspections are annual point-in-time checks and the multi-layered compliance program includes education, training, and reminders.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney on whether violations could have been caught earlier

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman, and thank you, Commissioner, for your thoughtful testimony.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: testimony, your work to contain this outbreak, and your commitment to doing better next time.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to echo some of the concerns that have already been raised, including enforcement, transparency, and that includes updating the website to reflect the accuracy of what this outbreak included.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Every life should be counted.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to go back to what was raised around enforcement and the violations that increased after in the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Were the violations that were uncovered during this outbreak response things that the department believes could or should have been identified earlier through the routine inspections that are already in place?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And if so, what needs to change about our routine inspections so that we find these problems before there is an outbreak?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me speak to the violations and give some detail there and then turn it over to Deputy Commissioner and talk a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So 110 violations were identified as part of this in that cluster region.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This stratified into different sort of types of violations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: 15 of them were public health hazards, 50 of them were critical violations, and then another 40 were general violations found in this cluster region.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So let me turn it over to Deputy Commissioner Crenshaw.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the inspections that we do, it's part of our cluster responses because we're also trying to understand what has happened during a cluster.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But I want to just note that the inspections, which as we've talked about, is one piece of our overall enforcement program, which includes that outreach, education, training.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Those are designed to be an annual inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it's really a point-in-time check to promote compliance along with all of the other things that we do.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And it's really...

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The constant monitoring and maintenance that the owners have to do,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: that is the prevention that we need to reduce the risk of Legionella bacteria growing in these systems, which are an ideal environment for the growth of Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So in these cases where issues were uncovered, why weren't they discovered earlier through these inspections that you were talking about, and what can we do in the future to find those problems?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We aim to conduct an annual inspection, and when we conduct that inspection, if we find violations, we will issue a summons.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: All of that is designed to provide, we have multiple points in our overall program to

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: encourage cooling tower operators to follow the very detailed requirements in the laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I quickly wanted to speak about the frequency of the requirements and particularly in the summer when we know cooling systems are heavy.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks about best practices for scheduling inspections ahead of summer and raises concerns about Intro 1006 implementation. Martin and Schiff explain existing cleaning requirements and caution that excessive biocide use can corrode systems and promote bacteria growth.
chapters.title: Council Member Maloney on Intro 1006 cleaning frequency and summer best practices

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: relied upon, what are some of the best practices around scheduling, phasing, and redundancy ahead of summer months so we can catch these violations before the outbreak begins, and wanting to learn a bit more

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: more about intro 1006 and your concerns there with the implementation.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We want to increase the frequency, but make these practical.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me start with intro 10006 and then hand it to Deputy Commissioner Schiff on the first part of that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So I think the term cleaning can mean a number of different things.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so I think we're eager to follow up with you to really get into some of the details there.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But for instance, if we were to define cleaning as doing more of the hyperhalogenation, which is applying that caustic

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: and corrosive material, that biocide, it can actually wear out the inside of the metal, which then potentially creates more Legionella infestation and contamination in the cooling tower.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So there are ways of doing cleaning that can reduce that risk.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So getting into the details is probably the next best step.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it over to Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: There's a couple of ways to think about your question.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: First is that the law that the council has enacted and then the regulations that we have issued set out very, very specific timing and frequency of certain kinds of monitoring and maintenance activities.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And it is literally some things have to happen three times a week.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Some things have to happen weekly, monthly, biannually, annually.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But also, critically, every cooling tower operator is required to develop its own protocol.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And monitoring and maintenance plan that is specific to its cooling tower and its cooling tower system and how it operates in its building and what are the requirements for that particular system to maintain it.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the system, we want the system to remain in balance.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So that is why we require a visual inspection at certain points, ongoing biocide at other times, and

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: the operators are collecting multiple indicators to see if their monitoring and maintenance plan is working to keep that system in balance and reduce the risk that that bacteria is going to grow

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: and to do that monthly sampling so that if it is growing, they will catch it early.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We know that this bacteria can grow quickly.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They catch it early.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They may catch it at a later stage, and depending on what those sample results show, if that bacteria is growing, there's very specific details on the corrective action that they're required to take, the confirmatory sampling timing,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: and ongoing remediation if it doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I will say that the schedule that we have set out as the default schedule is based in the scientific literature.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It is the best practice and what the evidence shows us are our best practices.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We are, and they apply year-round, but there are some additional, there is one additional

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: precautionary measure that we require owners to take during the summer because we know that there is additional risk and that is for that hyperhalogenation that the commissioner mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me just share one more piece of information as an update to the council.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Council member you referenced the

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: website not including the 11 deaths it does include the 11 deaths it was updated last week

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: the information basically that we get comes in as you heard from dr howard when we can get it when we can verify it and when we have that information we update the site and so it is updated now

chapters.summary: Council Member Morano questions why it took a deadly outbreak and public exposure to get 97% compliance, asking why non-compliant buildings weren't publicly identified before people got sick. Martin says the law was only eight weeks old and transparency is now a core strategy.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano on compliance jump and public pressure as enforcement tool

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're going to ask Councilmember Murano, who's on virtually, to ask questions because in order for somebody to ask questions virtually, we have to have quorum, so we have quorum now.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So, Councilmember Murano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair, and I want to thank the Commissioner and his whole team, but also all the families that spoke out about a situation that I'm sure was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, in your testimony, I want to touch upon a few of the areas that you

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: that you brought up.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Namely, your testimony says that before the Upper East Side cluster, that citywide compliance with the new monthly Legionella testing requirement was only

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: 74% thereabout.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And then there was this jump to 97%, according to your testimony, two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And you specifically call public pressure and transparency.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One of your most effective enforcement tools.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why did it take a deadly outbreak and public exposure to get owners to comply at that level?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If publicly identifying non-compliant buildings works, why weren't you doing

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: that before people got sick?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: This law was eight weeks old.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The ink was barely dry on it when we first started this cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That citywide compliance rate was 77%, and 74% was the compliance rate

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: in that region.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: What we learned from this experience is with this brand new law, right, having transparency be a core piece of this, a way that we promulgate the law,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: needs to be front and center to get to the compliance rates that we want, that New Yorkers deserve.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And so you better believe for every single one of those cooling tower operators that were not compliant, we held them accountable.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That also is reflected in the new measure that we announced yesterday, leveraging what we learned in this cluster with compliance to make it easier for New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: to check their cooling tower on their building to see how compliance is going and to map that information for them.

chapters.summary: Morano questions the jump from zero summonses in May-June to 180 in July, and asks why DOB-DOHMH data cross-referencing wasn't routine before two clusters involving unregistered towers. Martin says the system improves with each cluster experience.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano on zero summonses before July and DOB data cross-check

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
