utterances.text: Council staff also found that in the three zip codes that became the outbreak area, the Department of Health issued zero cooling tower summonses in May, zero in June, and then 180 in July.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What changed in July?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What did the city suddenly start looking for after people were already sick?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We, as a...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: mentioned issued over 100 violations in this cluster region.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Many of those were public health hazards.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Many of them were critical violations.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But I also want to share that the violations that we issue are just one layer in a multi-layered system that helps to keep

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: New Yorkers safe and reduce the risk of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The first two layers are what the owners must do.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: They must do daily, weekly, and monthly actions.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: They must, as the second layer, submit their Legionella sampling to us.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And the third layer is we actually go and investigate.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So these three layers are all happening at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The fourth layer, as you've described, the corrective actions and the fines, are certainly one piece of the puzzle, but it's not the full picture.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Finally, your testimony says the administration will now cross-reference DOB and health department records to identify unregistered cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You also acknowledge the city already has the capacity to do that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why wasn't that basic data cross-check already routine before this outbreak?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why did it take two Legionnaires clusters involving unregistered towers for the administration to implement it?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Because strong systems can improve when they identify new ways to do things better.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And we identified in 2025 that an unregistered cooling tower was at the source of that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We immediately put that knowledge into place in practice in 2026 and picked up an unregistered cooling tower at the start of the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But we want to now formalize that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We want to make it automatic.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We want to have the systems talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: New Yorkers shouldn't have to depend on

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: staff members across two different agencies working together to figure this out.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We should have systems that are automatically doing this work on the back end.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Council member, council member now.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Council member, we went over already.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have to go to other members.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay, I'd love to be in the second round just for one brief comment as well.

chapters.summary: Council Member Won asks about notifying hotel guests when Legionella is detected and protecting workers from retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions. Schiff describes the Highline Hotel case as an example of the system working, and notes 311 as the reporting mechanism.
chapters.title: Council Member Won on hotel Legionella notification and worker protections

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So, Council Member Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Last month, near-critical rates of Legionella were found at a hotel in my district.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What measures does DOHMH have in place for notifying guests at hotels ahead of, during, and after their stays when there are critical or near-critical rates of Legionella that are detected at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So one thing to make clear right up front is that the towers are consistently tested,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: sampled, and owners have a very clear understanding of what needs to happen at what rate of Legionella bacteria that's found.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: In the water.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So for instance,

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: at a rate of 10 CFUs or colony forming units, they need to remediate.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: If it goes higher, there are next actions that need to be taken.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it to Deputy Commissioner Crenshaw to talk a little bit more about the highline situation.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Yes, I think we know the hotel you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And it's actually a great example of how the system is working.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We had done an inspection, a routine inspection there, and taken a sample at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It was non-detect, no evidence of Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Soon thereafter, the operators of that cooling tower took their own sample and did find levels of Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They remediated that initial, it was a low level, that initial remediation was not effective.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Their compliance sampling and testing showed that there was more work for them to do.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They did that additional corrective action, and then they found that they had killed that bacteria, and they were back to that non-detect level.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So that was actually, to me, that was a great example of the new regime that the council had put in place for that monthly sampling, doing exactly what we wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So if they, as a scenario where, you know, an employer does not do what they're supposed to do, what measures are there to hold employers accountable when workers, you know, particularly those with pre-existing health conditions,

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: which make them especially vulnerable, are put in direct contact?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: with critical Legionella concentrations.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I also should add that, and this goes to some of the questions that the chair was asking,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: the levels of bacteria in the cooling towers when we require remediation, that doesn't mean that those are an immediate risk for a cluster.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We know that the bacteria is going to grow in these systems, and when those sample results come back showing some growth, what that means is that the owner needs to adjust its maintenance and monitoring plan, take corrective action, see what's out of balance.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If those bacteria levels are growing, they maybe need to take a harder look and make those adjustments.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The council's law does say that owners are required when asked to provide that information, and I think that was one of the things we clarified for the owners here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Chair, can I ask one quick question?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How can workers report any unsafe conditions related to Legionnaires and ensuring that they won't face any type of retaliation?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Is there a tip line, anonymous tip line, or anything like that that DOHMH operates?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They can call 311.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And I will say that owners are always welcome to call us and to do technical assistance, as we did in this case with the Highline.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We are here to provide guidance and TA.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wong criticizes the mayor's absence from the affected community, contrasting with previous mayors who visited outbreak areas. He questions the adequacy of public outreach and social media messaging about symptoms and testing.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong on mayor's absence and public outreach concerns

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is not my first encounter Legionnaires outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is, in my memory, the third one.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And during the previous Legionnaires outbreaks, I've seen Mayor de Blasio, I've seen Mayor Adams personally went into the affected communities, held multiple in-person press conferences and spoke directly to residents.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that's one thing I have not seen doing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I remember Mayor Adams even drank the tap water on camera in Harlem to reassure people that the water is safe.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is there anything being done to assure the public that the water is safe, or from you or from the mayor's office?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you talk about that?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: First, thank you for the question, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: When it comes to building investigations, where there again is a potential Legionella contamination in the potable water supply, it is safe to drink the water.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So I want to set that record straight, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: If there are other areas that you have specifically in mind, we're happy to talk about those.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I think public outreach is important because if a tower is contaminated, I think it's the Department of Health's job to inform the people working there or the people visiting there.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That may be exposed to Legionnaires.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And if you are in the risk group, you should be tested or you should go see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because they may treat this as a regular summer cold or whatever it is, and then they may just stay home and rest rather than, oh, this is serious, I need to get myself tested.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I've been hearing since 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That, oh, you're testing the water towers, you're testing your Patriot dish.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But where is the outreach?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: To the office workers in this tower that you tested positive.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You know, we tested the AC towers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You know, I don't see any, I've been searching.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I haven't seen any social media postings.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I haven't seen any videos.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I found videos of the mayor talking about the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We're talking about the gold cards, talking about Netanyahu, but nothing about Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Has anything been done?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is there any videos, social media postings on that?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because we cannot just keep testing water towers and then not telling the public you have to get tested.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I disagree with your assertion, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We have been putting communications at the core of our response.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: To talk about social media for a second, 2.2 million impressions for this cluster with the social media content that we put out.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: 15 in total community presentations, three town halls.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I myself was in the community doing the canvassing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Let me tell you my experience, okay?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: As a visitor to the Met Museum, I've been there twice, one for the Raphael exhibit in May and one for the Revolution exhibit in July.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I went there with my wife.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: She came back sick.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I have not got a single notice from the Met Museums that we've been tested for Legionnaires.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please get yourself tested.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And those are the concerns that I have because we could potentially, a lot of people may get sick if they visit the Met Museum and the cooling towers are infected.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I'm sorry to hear about your wife, and I hope she's feeling better.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: She was sick two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And how's she doing now?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: She's doing okay now, but she's young.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But these are the concerns I have that you've got to tell the public that if you are this group of people and you have these symptoms, go.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong, if you have a question, that's fine, but this is not a back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'll save it for round two.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me just respond to that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We have been doing that messaging.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We did that messaging throughout the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Again, radio ads throughout the region, over 180, two tabling events, 10 canvassing events.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Our job was to get the message out, and we delivered on that job, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: A council member questions whether early testing helps and raises concerns about low-income New Yorkers without providers. Dr. Howard emphasizes testing is only recommended for symptomatic individuals and that H&H provides care regardless of insurance or immigration status.
chapters.title: Council Member on early testing access for low-income New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Stein?

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: Thank you, and I really thank you for your information and the work you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: Does early testing help if someone's contracted Legionella, Legionnaires?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Testing is incredibly important when it comes to Legionnaires disease, and it also is multifaceted.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There's testing that needs to happen with urine.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: There's testing that needs to happen with x-rays and imaging, with blood testing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Which testing are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: So early testing.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: So you're saying people getting tested earlier that they might be exposed is good for them because then we can have a medical response after getting tested, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: It's important to do early testing and also to connect people to the referring provider to then take the results of that test and make it action.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: And you are aware that not every New Yorker, especially low-income New Yorkers, have providers, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: And so in a situation, especially in a lower-income area, if a provider, if the people who are potentially exposed to Legionella don't have a medical provider, they're at a disservice unless the government steps in and provides that support, right?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, let me hand it over to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Howard to share a little bit more from this.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Commissioner, and thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: I just want to commend you for your interest in ensuring that New Yorkers have access to health care.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: This is a very important issue.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: I also want to clarify that in terms of testing for Legionnaire's disease, that is indicated when a person has symptoms suggested of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: It is not a disease that we just screen for in people that do not have symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: So people who are elderly or people with disabilities or immune compromised,

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: earlier testing for them, especially if we know that they've been exposed, can prevent from what we've heard from the tragedies that have happened this year in New York.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Although the groups that you just stated, those who are elderly, those who are immunocompromised, those who have underlying medical conditions such as chronic lung disease, are at increased risk of developing Legionnaire's disease,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Legionnaire's testing is only recommended if they have symptoms suggested of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Legionnaire's disease is not COVID.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: There is no benefit to doing a screening test, okay?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And as an infectious disease doctor, I do not support blanket screening for Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: There's no clinical benefit.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: There's no public health benefit.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: So you're saying for people who are exposed, who are compromised, who might have some symptoms, but they may be concerned or non-concerned, testing could assist those people.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: That's different than blanket screening, but you're saying there is a population that early testing could have.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: assist, especially to get them the help that they needed earlier.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Anyone who has symptoms suggestive of Legionnaire's disease needs prompt evaluation by a clinician.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: So we agree with that, right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And that would include a clinical evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And the ordering of diagnostic tests for Legionnaire's disease, as well as other illnesses that can present similar to Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Now, those are best done in a health care setting.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: For folks who don't have access, though, having remote services like we do in H&H all the time, we take a show van and we get people on the street to get access to services.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: We do remote services because we meet people where they're at, because especially people with compromised immune systems or people who are fearful, having remote accesses or local accesses is helpful for them

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: because they may not have a health care provider that they have connected to.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Yeah, so you mentioned H&H.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And as you know, H&H provides clinical services to all New Yorkers without regard to their insurance status or their immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And that was part of our messaging, as well as the fact that they could call 311 and be connected with a health care provider.

utterances.speaker: Council Member
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Narcisse criticizes the failure to learn from Harlem and fill positions, and suggests posting cooling tower test results in buildings like elevator and restaurant inspection grades. Martin agrees there's merit to the idea and notes the new transparency measures.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse on staffing failures and building posting requirements

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner and your team for being here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair and Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What we have seen in Harlem, we did not learn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: All what we do as medical professional, which you're a doctor, it's, I don't want anyone to die on my shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's what I would say all the time in the ER.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: No one should die, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I know you not taking it lightly because as a physician and your team is to prevent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But what I don't understand, why that...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We had shorter staff, and I heard it from my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So why we never address that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because we did not learn, and our whole life is to prevent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We did not learn from what took place in Harlem to make preventative approach to prevent people from dying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's what bothers me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think we need to do much more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I heard it from the speaker and, of course, from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I have some suggestions and some bills that maybe, because local

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: law 159 requires building owners to test their cooling towers for Les Journées every 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: one days and disinfect them during the summer month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But that information go up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So now we posted an elevator inspection certificate where everyone can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we post restaurant letters, grades and everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Why we not doing that in a building to let folks know when

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the building been tested and what's the result?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because people want to take charge of their health.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So first let me respond to the piece around staffing.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I disagree with your assertion, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We do have 56 total budgeted positions for these water ecologists.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: 50 of them are filled at this moment.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So we do have six staff that we're hoping to bring in.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And if you have recommendations, we would love to have the right person in one of those slots.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Now, to talk about your idea, I think there's absolutely merit to your idea.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: And I think we should consider, we should follow up and talk about the details of that.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: You see what we're doing with regard to transparency is moving in the direction that you're describing, right, with the revamping and relaunching of our public website so individuals

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: can put their address in and get a mapped feature of how their tower compares to others in their building with regard to Legionella sampling and Legionella history.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So I think that there's certainly...

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: conversation we had around this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I put the bill in and I would like to see it happen because people need to take one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What is the average cost to clean a cooling tower?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And what is the average cost to disinfect a cooling tower?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And what factors this cost?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, that can depend on a whole range of factors, but it's in the thousands of dollars to clean a cooling tower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I have more questions, but we need to make sure that we hire those folks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have 51 council members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You can send it to us, and we can promote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So make sure that we have enough staffing so we can not say sorry to those that lost their life and their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Aldebol questions when the 23 new positions were filled, challenges in hiring, and whether recruitment is effective. Martin explains the specialized civil service requirements and Schiff notes the difficulty finding qualified candidates with specific science credentials.
chapters.title: Council Member Aldebol on water ecologist hiring challenges and timelines

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Council Member Aldebar.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and Speaker Menon and Commissioner for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So you said you had 23 new positions funded November of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: When were the majority of those positions filled?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You said the positions are filled today, but how long did it take you to actually fill those positions?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yep, the majority of those positions were filled before this cluster started.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We can get you the exact dates of those over the course of the several months prior to the close.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And you still have six positions that remain to be filled in this particular job title, the water ecologist title?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what have been the challenges in hiring for those titles?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I would say the most important challenge is the fact that these are highly specialized, highly skilled positions.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: The requirements are that these folks have to have, for instance, a master's degree or potentially a BA with 24 credits plus related experience.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So these are highly skilled, highly specialized positions.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So it's not just about finding any person for these slots.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We have to find the right person for these slots.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is it possible that...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: folks could be hired in these positions and receive additional training.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: To get them certified?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Does the Department of Health provide colleges, universities with

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: these specific criteria for these jobs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So of course we do provide training once the staff start to be able to do the cooling tower inspections, but I think you're asking something different.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You're asking about looking to colleges to

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: to qualify people to be able to apply for these jobs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And it's such an important point that we need more people going into the sciences to be able to do these jobs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But as the commissioner said, these are the civil service requirements, either to have a master's degree in very specific areas of the sciences or a BA in those same areas with prior work experience.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So that is the challenge.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I will say we would welcome your help in getting the word out that we are recruiting.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It is a great job.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We have a mission-driven, wonderful team, and we have some more positions to fill.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Yeah, not so easy because I don't know too many water ecologists kind of running around my neighborhood who are looking for this job.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: But I think...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I think it requires a discussion about the qualifications and how, you know, is the recruitment for these positions effective enough?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because just putting something in LinkedIn is not going to get you there, right?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I think the other question that I have, if I may, Chair, what other positions are critical to the management of Legionella?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are you seeking to expand those job positions?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are there vacancies in those positions currently?

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll speak to the first, which is a new addition from last year, and then I'll hand it to Deputy Commissioner Dr.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Howard to talk a little bit about the laboratory work.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: But the community health workers that we were able to deploy as part of this cluster were, from my perspective, very critical.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: We had these community health workers out there within 48 hours on the Upper East Side engaging with residents, with individuals.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: I was out there with them doing some of the canvassing and talking to residents.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: So that was critical when it comes to managing these clusters.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Let me hand it to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Commissioner Martin
utterances.text: Howard.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So we have epidemiologists that do the surveillance for Legionnaire's disease as well as other diseases and also do the case investigations.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And then on the laboratory side, we have a wide range of staff that do the actual testing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: testing of the cooling tower samples, which includes the PCR testing and the culture testing, and then the whole genome sequencing and analysis.

chapters.summary: Council Member Ariola criticizes the mayor's absence and asks whether two Harlem DOH buildings are fully staffed with stationary engineers and in compliance with fire and building codes for cooling tower maintenance. Martin says they will follow up on specifics.
chapters.title: Council Member Ariola on mayor's absence and DOH building compliance

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember Areola.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You know, earlier today, I was listening to the testimony of Valerie Massim from Community Board 8, and she testified that Mayor Mamdani did not visit the area

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: where 94 people became sick with Legionnaire's disease and 11 died of the same disease.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I sat there, I listened, and I could not believe the horror in her voice that the mayor's absence was so obvious during a life-threatening, life-taking crisis

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: in his city, and yet he did not show up.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Why didn't he show up?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: He certainly was available because he was performing for the cameras to say that he was going to arrest Bibi Netanyahu when he came here to New York City, which turned out to be false.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So he wasted his time and the people of this city's residents'time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: By not giving them the personal attention they deserved for this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And thankfully, the speaker

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: this chair, this committee, and this body would not do the same.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Question.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are both the new DOH building at 40 West 137th Street and 2238 5th Avenue, both located in Harlem,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: fully staffed and in compliance with the New York City Fire Code and the building code with stationary engineers that are responsible for the operations and maintenance and water treatment of the cooling towers and air conditioning systems?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Let me get to your second question in a second, but first let me start with a response to the initial statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The mayor has been and was from the beginning involved in this cluster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We spoke every single day during this cluster.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, I don't really want to use up time on this, but he wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And that's where he should have been, not trying to fool the residents of New York City thinking that he could have Bibi Netanyahu arrested when there were people dying in this city.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That's where he should have been.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The question was these two specific buildings and the inspection history.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are they fully staffed in compliance with the New York City Fire Code and Building Code with stationary engineers that are responsible for operations and maintenance and water treatment of the cooling system, towers, and air conditioning systems?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're going to get back to you on the details on those two specific buildings, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so do you know that the stationary engineers who operate these

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Machines are responsible for checking the water treatment logs and testing required by the DOH is part of their job as their civil service description provides.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The buildings that you're describing, I'm not sure which buildings you're describing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're going to get back to them in details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If they have towers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you know how you could answer that?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: One more moment?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is if Assistant Commissioner John Beattie was here to testify, because he's in charge of those operations, and he's in charge of that maintenance of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And why isn't he here to answer questions like that?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Because those are very important questions to ask moving forward to make sure that Legionnaire's disease does not have additional outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: These answers should be able to be given to us today.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But again, the mayor's office has failed to have the proper people at the dais answering questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Councilmember, we have the right people here able to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We will get back to you on the details of those two specific buildings.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: These questions should be able to be answered now, and I thank you for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Salaam questions what is different about the department's approach and whether the same urgency was applied to communities with recurring cases in previous summers. Martin says the protocol is systematic and geography-independent, and each cluster leads to improvements.
chapters.title: Council Member Salaam on proactive approach and equity across communities

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember Salam?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: You know, our constituents, they've been calling for a more proactive approach in identifying and addressing potential sources of Legionella.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: The question still remains, and that is, is what has been actually, is what has been done actually solving the problem?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: We've been told that this is a preventable illness, but yet decade after decade, we still see our people dying.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: My question is what specifically is different about the department's approach in response to the Upper East Side today?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And why was that level of urgency not applied to the communities that experienced recurring cases in previous summers?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And also,

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: As you know, we passed legislation calling for water tower inspections in coordination with the Department of Buildings to be inspected more.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And why hasn't the city moved with greater urgency in implementing that mandate?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And lastly, how many water towers and other potential high-risk water systems have been inspected in the affected communities?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And how many have not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The answer is that we apply a systematic protocol to our cluster response, and that protocol does not depend on geography.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: zip code, our neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We apply the protocol that we have that the system demands, that the cluster demands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And yet, every time we do this, Councilmember, we identify ways to improve our already strong system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so every single cluster that we have,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: we learn something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have that experience, then improve and enhance our process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so the enhancements that you identified this time, again, we ran the most aggressive cluster we ever have, moving the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: full remediation to the PCR step, not waiting the two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We had the most transparent cluster we've ever had, not waiting the two weeks for the culture results before we shared the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We responded quickly and immediately in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the bottom line is every time we do this, we enhance and improve our process.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin reiterates that her data shows 21 positions unfilled during the outbreak and asks about the discrepancy. She also raises the June 23 vs. June 27 first case date discrepancy. Martin agrees to follow up with exact numbers, and Dr. Howard explains backfilling of case data.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin on water ecologist vacancy data discrepancy and case date confusion

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: She has a line of questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I just have one last question, but before asking the question, I know Councilmember Narcisse had to leave, but just one response, again, on this water ecology issue that Councilmember Narcisse raised.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I just, again, want to make clear.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That her line of questioning and my line of questioning are about, again, why heading into the summer months those positions weren't filled.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's what we're trying to talk about, the fact that 21 positions remained open as we head into the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So good that now, after this outbreak,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: position that we can fill, but we never should be in a position where heading into a time when we know that there's going to be these types of Legionnaires outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we want to make sure that every single one of these positions is filled moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I do have one last question.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I wanted to ask

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There was a press release that the health department put out around the second, when the second death unfortunately occurred.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And in that press release, it listed the first cases as June 27th and June 29th.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But if you go to the agency's Legionnaires webpage right now, it shows that the first case was all the way back on June 23rd.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: which would have been the date the patient's sample was collected.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I'm not sure how long it would have taken for that person to have tested positive for Legionella, but that's more than a week before the agency mobilized that outreach.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we wanted to understand why is there this discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, both great questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Let me just say a few words about the Watery College's position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Again, and then hand it over to Dr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Howard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Madam Speaker, the majority of those positions were filled before this cluster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I completely agree with your point that right now, 50 out of 56 positions filled and onboarded as a strong sign and signal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the majority of the positions that we needed were filled before this cluster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We can get you the exact numbers in a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Secondly...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, I would appreciate that because that's not what our data shows.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Our data shows that during the outbreak, only 35 of 56 authorized water ecologist positions were staffed.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: 21 were not staffed with active inspectors when the city needed that workforce the most.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So that's what our data shows.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So there seems to be a discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we would...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We can follow up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then to the second question, yeah, so this question is really about sort of...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: How do we and when do we count a case?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the process that we take prospectively, right, is to do interviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: with patients that are part of the affected region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And they tell us, for instance, when their symptoms started or when they began feeling sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's one clock that we're looking at, symptom onset as a clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's another clock, though, and that is the lab testing, so the actual diagnosis date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So these two clocks can be going at different times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm going to hand it to Dr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Howard to talk a little bit about backfilling, which can happen with these clocks.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So thank you, Commissioner, and thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So as one of our public health duties, the health department receives reports of infectious diseases

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: in New York City and routinely analyzes our surveillance data to identify a possible cluster of cases in space and time that would indicate a shared potential source of exposure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So there's approximately 200 to 600 cases of Legionnaire's disease in the city on an annual basis.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Each reported case is analyzed, including a review of the medical records and then a patient interview to get information about the source of exposure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And the protection we have in New York City is very robust.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We run sophisticated data analyses on a daily basis to identify clusters.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: In this instance, the cluster was identified by astute epidemiologists even before that data analysis system detected a signal.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And we acted very, very rapidly, as you've heard in today's testimony.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And this is really public health at its best.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Now, as time, so we only had a handful of unverified cases at the time that we announced there was a cluster of disease on the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Now, over time, we're doing the investigations of all these reports that we get in to determine whether someone is

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: spent time in the area during their period of exposure.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Often that can take some time, particularly if it's someone who worked or visited the area, worked in or visited the area, didn't live in the area,

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: if that person is hospitalized, if that person visited from another jurisdiction, we get that information

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: in a delayed fashion.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And then we add cases to our case count.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And in some instances, they might have had an earlier diagnosis date than those initial cases that we first identified through our surveillance system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker.

chapters.summary: Schulman presents data showing one-third of positions unfilled as of July 21 and asks whether vacancies were due to recruitment or OMB not releasing funding. Martin says 50 of 56 are now filled, and Dr. Howard confirms OMB issues are not in play and the challenge is recruitment.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on water ecologist vacancies during cluster and OMB funding

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I have a bunch of questions, but I'm just going to go once to quick round for my colleagues because I can stay here.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can I just, so I have a better understanding about, so with Legionnaires, obviously the towers are affected, but the plumbing system is impacted too, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The virus isn't just staying in the tower, it's going through the plumbing infrastructure, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The water infrastructure, going to the hoses, going to the faucets, going to the drains, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The bacteria is in the potable water system, which can be the plumbing in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so when you're testing, are you testing just the tower or are you testing the system too?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So these are two separate types of investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What we've been talking about so far has been what you've just referenced, which is us testing the cooling tower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What's going on at Haven Plaza, as you know, is a separate and distinct type of investigation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you're testing the plumbing system as well?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's actually only the plumbing system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And let me hand it to Deputy Commissioner Prince to explain a little more.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: I want to make sure I'm understanding your question.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that when we're testing, right, and sometimes we find the bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Present in the towers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We also

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Then what are we doing about making sure the plumbing, the system itself, when the water's coming to the faucet, is being tested as well?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So these are completely different.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And we are directed either to the cooling tower or to a building's internal plumbing system based on the information that is coming from our epidemiologists.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So as you've heard, there are a few hundred cases every year of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: The bacteria are everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: People are exposed all the time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And there are a few hundred cases every year.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Most of those cases we consider sporadic.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: The case investigators are following up.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: They don't know where the exposure is coming from.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: When they're seeing patterns in space and time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That's telling us that that bacteria may be growing in the built environment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And the kind of space and time pattern is what tells us which built environment is at risk.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: When we are seeing, as we saw on the Upper East Side, many cases in a short period of time, here our astute epidemiologists identified it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Very early, they could see what was coming even before, as you heard Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Howard say, our automated systems picked up on it.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: The typical community cluster pattern is many cases in a short period of time in a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That tells us that there is a cooling tower or could be multiple cooling towers where the bacteria is growing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: It enters.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: the environment as mist and spreads all over that neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We're not testing the potable water system because we know that that's coming from cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If it's in the tower and spreading it, you're saying it's not spreading through the water system.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And that's why we're not...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That's why there's no recommendation about showering.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: It's never about drinking water.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: It's completely different.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But when you're testing the tower and you find the bacteria in a building, like you mentioned Haven Plaza, then you're testing the water system.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: To the water's coming out of the faucet.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Yes, and let me return to the pattern, because we're seeing a very different kind of pattern when the clues are telling us to look at that potable water system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: The pattern that Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Howard's team is observing there is two cases as opposed to many.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Over a 12-month period, as opposed to very quickly, with a shared hot water system, as opposed to a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And so there that's telling us that what we suspect is the built environment that is at risk is that internal plumbing system.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That's where the sampling happens.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That's the community at risk.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And that's when we start talking about reducing risk if you are in a risk group by not taking a shower.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Never about drinking water because this is about inhalation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right, so I'm just saying when you're testing the water that's coming out of the faucet, I think your distinction you're making is a really important distinction, but to the

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: the public, right, it is really hard to understand.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And to the public, it is hard to communicate this information.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so if you're testing a tower or testing water coming out of the faucet for the bacteria, people have to have information and then need to know when they need to get help and what the signs are of illness.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I think what we're trying to say is I think

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: While you are experts in this and you've been trained in this, the public at large is not.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And English might not even be their first language.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So they need help and support.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And that's what we're trying to get.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm not saying you're not all working hard, but we're saying we're not getting that information out to people in a way that's helpful to provide them support when they're scared and not knowing what to do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Very quick.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'll be really quick.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We've been here since 10 a.m., and I'm still, I did not hear from anybody in this panel.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What are the symptoms of Legionnaire's disease?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe I covered those in my earlier testimony, and I will reiterate them here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're flu-like symptoms, things like cough, fever, shortness of breath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: These are the signs and symptoms of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And how would an individual distinguish that, oh, that's Legionnaires, I have to go see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or, oh, I should stay home in my bed and just rest a few days.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Where's the...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: distinction?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the distinction is embedded in the communications that we are giving, the targeted radio ads, the tabling events, the community presentations, the town halls, the press releases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: All of these are efforts, interventions to educate the public to not look past these symptoms because this is not potentially just a normal flu or a normal or a COVID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: This can be deadly, as we have seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's why it's critically important to do the communications as we have.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well, like back to my visit to the Met Museum, as someone who's been there, I should have been informed that, oh, we tested positive.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please look for these symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And if you have these symptoms, go see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have not got these notices.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I do not know whether you've sent them out to buildings that are tested positive with legionnaires in the AC tower.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So that is a question I want to know.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Have you done these outreaches?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or was it Office of Mass Engagement is doing that?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or they knock on doors or attend residence meetings?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is this something that you do?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or is it like the Office of Mass Engagement did?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We knocked on doors as part of our community health worker team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I knocked on dozens of them myself there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But to your broader question around the communications to the building owners, that's why our

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: our work with you all and the relationships that we have with you at City Council is so important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We did eight elected briefings to have you all help us as well get the message out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We did three town halls, two press conferences with the mayor, nine press releases to get the word to these building owners to share this message as well.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That's done by Department of Health and not the Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We did that outreach at the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I have some questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So on the speaker talked about and other members talked about the infield, the water ecology positions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So the data is showing that as of July 21st, that one third.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Of the positions remained unfilled.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that was the issue that we've been trying to get to during the course of the hearing as to why they were still unfilled at that particular point in time when the outbreak was far along.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That was what we were asking, why they were unfilled at that point.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And then the question is,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Were they unfilled because you were still recruiting people, or were they unfilled because OMB wasn't releasing the funding for it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you exactly on that data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: make sure that we align there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I can tell you that at this moment of the 56 positions, 50 of them are filled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are six that are unfilled.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But we're just going to the, in the heart of the cluster.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: I can add that we've been working very closely with OMB and there are no, those issues are not in play.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Really, it is a challenging position to fill.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Local, you know what, out of curiosity, do you know what the pay level is in New York City versus other cities?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is it lower or higher?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because there are other agencies where we have that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we can look into that and circle back.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, a comparison between the cities?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we can look back and circle back to you.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how DOHMH prepared to implement and enforce her 2025 law requiring monthly cooling tower testing. Schiff describes updating guidance, developing regulations, sending notices, holding training sessions, and conducting outreach starting in late 2025.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on Local Law 159 implementation and enforcement preparation

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Local law 159, which was my law of 2025, went into effect in May of this year, requiring more frequent cooling tower testing and additional biocide treatment during warm weather conducive to Legionella growth.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How did DOHMH prepare to implement and enforce the bill leading up to its effective date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In many ways, in fact, the preparations happened long before the May 8th law was promulgated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Let me hand it to Deputy Commissioner Crenship to share more.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Yes, we began preparing for that May 8th effective date late in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We knew that there would be no grace period and we wanted the regulated

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: to be prepared to implement.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So in late 2025, we began updating the guidance on our website.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We would be letting the operators know that there was new information for them.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We developed the new detailed regulation to implement your local law chair.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We sent out notices when that regulation was open for comment.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That's an opportunity not only to gather comments from the regulated community, but it's also a time to notify them that this was coming.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We notified them again when it became final.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We held training sessions.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We sent out reminders.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: So there was a lot happening.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We started talking about it at inspections well before May 8th.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: And it is a new requirement.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We know that not everyone's going to be in compliance immediately upon an effective date, but we wanted as many people to be ready to go right on May 8th.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What additional outreach needs to be done ahead of the next cooling season to ensure greater compliance with local law 159?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We will be continuing.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: It's part of our, you know, the inspection is a, we think of it as a teachable moment, and we will be continuing to conduct education at the inspection and to do other ongoing outreach.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Owners will receive violations if they're not in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That is another way of providing them feedback and an incentive to comply.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What support does DOHMH need from other agencies or from the council to conduct outreach for building?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: owners and you should think about that and come back to us because we can obviously help with folks in our particular districts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a very good point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We will think about that in circle back.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about NYC's remediation threshold of 1,000 CFU/ml versus Toronto's 10, and whether lowering it would help. Martin and Schiff clarify that NYC also requires action at the 10 CFU level, matching Toronto's standard.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on remediation thresholds and comparison to Toronto standards

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Based on current DOHMH rules, full remediation including cleaning and hyperhalogenation.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is only required when Legionella culture results from a cooling tower indicate levels of the bacteria above a thousand CFU milliliters.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In Toronto, they do it at 10, which obviously is really low.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We do it at a really high.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you think that if we lowered that, that that would be helpful?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, let me say a few words and then hand it to Deputy Commissioner Corinne Schiff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: First of all, we are in communication with the team in Vancouver.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we are working closely to learn from them, and they are learning from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There is this question of what to do at the 10 CFU line when it comes to the bacteria levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We both agree, our system and Vancouver's system, that that needs to be treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that is what happens here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do demand and require that building owners treat at that 10 unit level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, things are not going untreated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But there is a difference beyond the treatment, and I'll hand it to Deputy Commissioner Kernship.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: I agree, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: The level that you just...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: referenced chair is the same level that we have here.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Our regulation has very detailed requirements for levels of Legionella bacteria and the corrective action that is required, and ours starts at that very same level that you have cited for Toronto.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Schulman questions a July 22 vacancy posting for a public health engineering consultant and asks how many staff are dedicated to Legionnaires prevention. Martin says they have public health engineers on staff and the majority of the environmental sciences division works on this issue.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman on public health engineer vacancy and environmental sciences staffing

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: During previous Legionnaires disease outbreaks, DOHMH has had a head public health engineer on staff to help with the agency's response.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: However, on July 22nd, DOHMH posted a vacancy for a public health engineering consultant in the Bureau of Environmental Sciences and Engineering.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When did DOHMH last have a public health engineer consultant on staff, and how long has the position been vacant?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We have public health engineers on staff.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
