utterances.text: That posting might have...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So what was the posting for?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: I'll have to let...

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: We have other positions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Howard
utterances.text: That we are hiring for.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many staff with the Environmental Sciences and Engineering Bureau are currently dedicated to Legionnaires disease prevention, including tower inspection, plan review, and related enforcement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, it's probably the whole, it's the majority of the people that are in that division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We can get you specific numbers in a more detailed way, but that is the full brunt of what that team is aiming to do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: There are other questions, but we'll do this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We'll send them to you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You'll send us back an answer.

chapters.summary: Schulman wraps up the Q&A portion, thanks the DOHMH team, and invites Assemblymember Wright and Senator Cleare to give testimony before opening public testimony.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman concludes Q&A and invites state legislators to testify

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So we're done with this portion.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank the team here for your time.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, we really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So, Assemblyman Wright?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Senator Clare.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I am now opening the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight topic and the legislation being considered.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank both the Assemblyman and the Senator for...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I know it was a long time and we were, we were,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You know, there were a lot of questions or a lot of issues, and I really apologize.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank you for being here.

chapters.summary: Assemblymember Jordan Wright describes Harlem's 2025 outbreak with 90 hospitalizations and 114 cases, emphasizing disproportionate impact on Black and brown communities. He discusses his state law requiring biannual cooling tower certification, 48-hour remediation, and increased fines.
chapters.title: Assemblymember Wright on Harlem outbreak and state cooling tower law

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So go ahead, Assemblyman.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Shulman, and I want to thank the whole committee for being present and allowing for transparency during this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: It's very important, and it's critical to all of our constituents.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: My name is Jordan Wright.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I represent the New York State Assembly 70th District, and that's central and west Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: And unfortunately, my neighbors and loved ones in this village that I grew up in,

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: been have experienced a deadly Legionnaires outbreak last summer.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: In Harlem, we lost 70 community members due to Legionnaires and more fell ill during that closer of this disease, with Harlem seeing 90 hospitalizations and at least 114 reported cases.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: It's a tale that we all know all too well.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Black and brown communities repeatedly serve as ground zero for tragedies like these, horrific and preventable public health failures.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: In 2026, in the greatest city in the world, it should no longer be the norm that when white folks get a cold, black folks get the flu.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: We all deserve to be healthy.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Here are some of what we in Harlem have learned from our ground zero.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Clear communication is key.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: The community deserves prompt and consistent updates from reliable sources.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: This is not only key to ensuring public trust and collaboration, it is essential to containing and eradicating any cluster or outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: In Harlem, I hosted regular briefings and engaged with community stakeholders day and night to ensure that the public was able to learn and adapt quickly to new facts.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: We ensured that necessary resources were widely available to our community throughout the situation and that any relevant or new information was shared promptly and widely in Harlem as best as we could.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Full transparency is the only acceptable way to navigate a public health event like Legionnaires.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Full transparency is how we prevent more illnesses.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: It's how we prevent death, because as we know, even one is too many.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Legionella bacteria and its

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: impact is well known and not uncommon.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: It should not take active cases and New York lives to bring it to the forefront of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: All New York communities, but certainly the black and brown communities that are so often battered by environmental inequalities, deserve the peace of mind that comes with strong public health regulations and the funding and enforcement to make the entire city healthier for all of our families.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Last month, the governor signed into law a bill that I sponsored with Senator Cordell Clear requiring that owners and operators of cooling towers in New York City

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: certify their cooling towers have been inspected, tested, cleaned, and disinfected in compliance with New York City administrative code.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: The bill also sets timelines for building owners to notify the New York City Department of Buildings and take steps to remedy any public health hazards in cooling towers and increases in civil

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: penalties on building owners who fail to report or address these issues and require biannual certifications.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Perhaps most importantly, the new law clarifies that the building owner must take steps to address maintenance deficiencies as soon as possible, but no later than 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: That's two days.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: It increases fines and penalties and modernizing a process that we can no longer afford to keep antiquated.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: This is not about whose plan outdoes the other.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: This is about saving lives.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: So thank you again for having me.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: I look forward to working together on all fronts to ensure the safety of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Jordan Wright
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman.

chapters.summary: Senator Cordell Cleare describes Harlem as ground zero for the 2025 outbreak and ongoing in-building Legionella cases at NYCHA Wagner Houses and 3333 Broadway. She urges advancing legislation on public education, tenant notification, and workforce barriers, and proposes a Legionnaires' Disease Prevention Act.
chapters.title: Senator Cleare on Harlem as ground zero and comprehensive reform needs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Senator?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and I want to thank.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and I want to thank Speaker Menon and Health Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Shulman, for holding this very important hearing, and all the council members here today united in the goal to keeping New Yorkers safe from Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I am New York State Senator Cordell Clear, Chair of the Aging Committee in the Senate, and proudly representing Central Harlem, East Harlem, El Barrio, West Harlem, and parts of the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Last summer, my wonderful district, District 30, which I also dear to my heart, was ground zero for the 2025 Legionnaires outbreak that claimed the lives of at least seven New Yorkers and infected hundreds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: More right in the heart of Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Legionella was unfortunately, has unfortunately remained a continual issue for the community since Harlem's first reported cases back in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: We saw it again in NYCHA's Wagner houses in November, followed shortly thereafter by one in January at 3333 Broadway, which is one of the largest residential developments in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: And for those residents specifically, the investigation has brought months of interrupted water access, diminished quality of life, and countless hours spent organizing with management to address the conditions in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: In both these investigations, though, Legionella was detected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: In hot water systems rather than cooling towers at the center of the summer outbreak, leaving residents

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: without reliable hot water during the coldest months of the year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Harlem has become a vanguard of sorts for organizing around and demanding responsiveness to how we maintain our buildings and strengthen the systems that keep New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: We are behind and playing catch up as warmer temperatures and more frequent periods of extreme heat associated with climate change create conditions that make Legionnaires disease more prevalent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Far too often, black and brown communities find themselves on the front lines of environmental health risks and bear the disproportionate burden of ecological vulnerabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: In response to the 2025 outbreak and our ongoing efforts, I was proud to introduce four bills, one that has now become law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I partnered with Assemblymember Jordan Wright in the State Assembly requiring biannual certification of cooling towers, proactive testing and inspection, remediation within 12 to 24 hours, and increased fines for violations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: But there's still more work to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I'm urging my colleagues to advance additional pieces of legislation that will strengthen public education and awareness campaigns and ensure that tenants and residents receive timely notice when a potential health threat is identified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I believe we should expand our capacity to test and inspect cooling towers while also examining the workforce barriers that make it difficult to recruit and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: or maintain adequate staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Based on information given to my office in real time, I don't know if the Department of Health, if the agency can confirm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I understand there's only been one violation written between last year and now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: That begs the question, are there enough qualified inspectors to meet the demands of the law?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Are qualification requirements unnecessarily limiting the pool of workers who could be trained and brought into these roles?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: We need to identify and remove unnecessary obstacles so that 100% oversight and compliance with these basic safety precautions is not simply the goal but the standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: And with all that we have learned from the deaths in Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: It's a greater tragedy that those people died in vain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I want to give the council credit for always responding on this issue, even though it continues to bedevil us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: You have passed legislation in the last decade that has improved certain aspects of Legionnaires'detection, and I'm encouraged that you have seven legislative introductions before you today that will make an even greater difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I fully support that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Lastly, I hope the council will support my comprehensive reform, which enacts the Legionnaires'

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Disease Prevention Act, a source-to-tap solution that will prevent and mitigate Legionella long before it gets into our cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I am confident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: that with decisive city and state action, we can create an environment that ends Legionella outbreaks, prevents the public from becoming the litmus test for Legionnaires,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: And these outbreaks, as we know them, put ourselves in the strongest possible position to finish this year with no additional outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I look forward to your partnership in this fight going forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Before you leave, Senator, I didn't realize that you're the chair of the Aging Committee.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I'm going to, I don't know if you've met with the new DFTA commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: And older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And, you know, getting them, like, information because they, you know, if they don't show up to a senior center, then you've got to go look for them and all this stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So she's somebody I used to work with and I know really well.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But I would ask, and one of the questions that we're going to send back to Department of Health is how they work with all the agencies, including Department for the Homeless and all of that, in terms of

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: coordination, especially when there's an outbreak, because that time period is very tight.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yes, it's very critical.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And Assemblyman...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you for all that you do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I think that, you know, we should all like really sit and work together.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're more than happy.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I am more than happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We have other folks, too, that are willing to work with us as well to help us with this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I look forward to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Me as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

chapters.summary: Gwen Hanlon describes her husband Kevin's death from Legionnaires in 2017 during the Lenox Hill outbreak, noting 96% of cases are sporadic and not part of outbreaks. She calls for comprehensive investigation of every case and a source-to-tap approach like New Jersey's.
chapters.title: Gwen Hanlon on husband Kevin's 2017 Legionnaires death and sporadic cases

utterances.text: Okay, we're going to resume public testimony.

utterances.text: The next panel is Robert Bocock, Kim Smith,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Hi, Chairman Shulman and members of the Health Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to share my story, my husband's story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: My name is Gwen Hanlon, and my husband, Kevin, died from Legionnaires in 2017.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: I've been begging for the prevention of Legionnaires for nine years, so please keep going, and thank you for doing this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: I've been doing it for nine years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Kevin died from Legionnaires, and New York City still cannot tell me where the bacteria that killed him came from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: He was diagnosed with lung cancer at 46 years old from 9-11 exposure, but lung cancer didn't kill Kevin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: We believe he was exposed to it during the Lenox Hill outbreak where he was receiving cancer treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Before Legionnaires, Kevin was active in responding well to treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: And like the previous victims, families explained, this is a horrible way to die.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: He was intubated, had extreme fever, agonizing pain, withdrawals from the meds, and was in a medically induced coma with a feeding tube and a tracheotomy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: And he fought like this for five weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: After five weeks, I had to tell my six- and nine-year-old children their dad was never coming back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: The Department of Health and the CDC did not report on my husband's death because he was considered a one-of case, and I have sought answers and records for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: I appreciate the focus on outbreaks, but you are missing thousands of victims.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: 96% of all cases are considered sporadic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: The proposed New York legislation must call for comprehensive investigation of every reported Legionnaire's case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: New York officials didn't address Kevin's case then, and here we are in the exact same area nine years later with a worse tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Thousands of more New Yorkers have become sick since Kevin's passing, and I'm still asking the same questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: I'm not a scientist, but there's some bright ones here today, and they are begging New York to focus on the source of the water.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: New York responds to outbreaks the same way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Identify a cluster, test cooling towers, and remediate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: And then we wait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: We wait for more cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Why isn't New York looking at the entire water system the way New Jersey did?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: In 2024, New Jersey passed what is described as the most comprehensive Legionnaires disease prevention law in the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: States like Pennsylvania and Maryland are following.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: So I have a new question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Why does New York continue to handle the outbreaks the same way for the past 10 plus years and expect a different outcome?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: It's not working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Nothing changes if nothing changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: I'm here today to ask for you to keep this going and make a change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Handle it differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Thank you for hearing our story, my husband's story, and thank you for doing more to make a change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gwen Hanlon
utterances.text: Maybe the story will be different next year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Upper East Side resident Jennifer Ratner questions why NYC isn't a model for Legionnaires prevention given its density and cooling tower count. She calls for broader discussion of biocide use and urges NYC to be an innovator rather than following existing approaches.
chapters.title: Jennifer Ratner urges NYC to be global innovator on Legionnaires prevention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: So my name's Jennifer Ratner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: I'm a 60-year-old long-term resident of the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: My dad is 86 and thankfully did not get Legionella, but lives in one of the buildings that was positive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: And I just want to start with a question I hope will be asked in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: So I hope that Legion...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: Legionnaires disease experts will be asking in the future, wow, how come New York City has so many cooling towers, dealing with 100 plus degree hot summers, is so densely populated, and yet

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: every summer there are no deaths from Legionnaires disease, or very few in New York City, which

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: We should be the model and not just be following along and to the previous testimony, not just doing kind of the same thing year after year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: I don't understand, you know, so there's prevention, and I really applaud your bill, which, you know, if enforced properly and some of the other bills will lead to more and more prevention moving forward so that we don't have the outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: But then during the outbreak, you know, the health department had up this sign right over there before that said, why is biocide not good?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: And they referred to the CDC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: I actually wrote to the Legionella team at the CDC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: Because it's very vague.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: Why couldn't we do, you know, we had just a small cluster, relatively few numbers of towers that were positive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: Why not just pull the samples and disinfect?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: I understand maybe you'll corrode the tanks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: But for, you know, a huge number of them, we were doing that anyway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: And, you know, waiting two days even for the PCR was probably too long in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: And I'm not an expert on it, but I think there should be much broader discussion and just not discount that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: And so I think we should be the innovators here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Ratner
utterances.text: So not just thinking about testing and preventing, but just be the innovators and be the model for the whole globe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Water treatment professional Bob Bocock presents independent sampling finding Legionella in 20% of Upper East Side building water fixtures. He argues cooling tower regulation alone is insufficient and calls for a comprehensive source-to-tap approach, noting NYC's unfiltered water status.
chapters.title: Bob Bocock on source-to-tap water system approach and unfiltered water

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Coleman and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Senate - Cordell Cleare
utterances.text: Bob, your mic.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Is that on?

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: I'll start back with thank you, Chair Shulman and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: My name is Bob Bocock.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: I am a licensed water treatment professional.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: For over 40 years, I've had experience in water utilities and water resource management.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: I was the state attorney general's expert witness in the Flint, Michigan case and work on water and water quality issues nationwide.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: I am a volunteer to the board for the Alliance for Prevention of Legionnaires Disease as their water quality advisor.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: First, I'd like to acknowledge the city's efforts in response to the Upper East Side outbreak, and our hearts go out to those who have been affected.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: who have been impacted and lost family members.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: As we look at what happened and the 94 cases and the 11 deaths associated with this outbreak, we need to ask a broader question.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: How do we prevent Legionnaire's disease before an outbreak occurs?

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Legionella is a waterborne organism.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: And preventing the disease requires looking beyond an individual exposure point.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: From my perspective as a water quality professional, we need to look at the entire water system from source through the public distribution system to building plumbing and the points

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: where the people are exposed rather than only treating one symptom of the underlying issues.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: The city's current approach is focused exclusively on cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Those systems are important, and they must be properly regulated and maintained.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: But cooling tower regulation alone is not comprehensive Legionnaires disease prevention.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: When found in the water, the Legionella in the tower is the same water that runs through the entire system, from the building, the municipal system, and serving the building's plumbing system.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: The Alliance conducted independent sampling in mid-July on the Upper East Side community affected by the Legionnaires'disease outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: That work found Legionella in multiple types of building water fixtures, including hose bibs outside closest to the water meter.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Over 20% of the samples

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: demonstrated very low chlorine residuals and high levels of Legionella.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Almost 20% of the samples'water systems in the Upper East Side in July were positive for Legionella.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: New York City currently has a...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I need you to summarize and then submit.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I will summarize.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: New York City, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: New York City currently has a filtration waiver from the federal government, meaning 90% of the drinking water in Manhattan is unfiltered.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: And until we take a concentrated approach that's systematic, that goes from source to tap, we're going to continue to be back here year after year.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, and please submit the rest of your testimony to us.

utterances.speaker: Bob Bocock
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

chapters.summary: Certified nurse midwife Patricia Loftman, testifying for the second year, says no new regulations are needed—what's required is monitoring and enforcement of existing laws. She argues fines cannot be imposed without adequate inspector staffing.
chapters.title: Patricia Loftman repeats last year's call for enforcement over new regulations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Greetings, Chairperson Truman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Thank you for this opportunity to provide testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: My name is Patricia Loftman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I am a certified nurse midwife.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I speak as the former midwifery service director at Harlem Hospital for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I also am a New York City resident who could be impacted by Legionella at any time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I testified almost one year ago on September 19th before this very committee on this very same topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Yet here I am again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I have attached a copy of my testimony from last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Last year, DOHMH proposed regulatory reforms to improve monitoring and accountability with the city law to prevent an outbreak, a legionary recurrence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Proposed changes included requiring cooling tower testing every 30 days instead of every 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: every 90, increasing fines for noncompliance as the penalty for noncompliance was just $2,000 for the first violation, followed by up to $10,000 for subsequent violations,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: hiring more inspectors and engineers, expanding proactive sampling capacity and creating neighborhood health centers to provide information during emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Cooling tower inspections, according to city experts, are a critical defense against Legionnaire outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Among the 10 buildings identified by DOHMH last year, all but one had cooling towers that were either behind on Legionella testing or had not been inspected by the city in the past year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: During my testimony last year, I stated that no new regulations were required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: What was required was monitoring and enforcement of existing laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I further stated that it was ludicrous to expect that requiring testing every 30 days instead of every 90 in the absence of inspector staffing numbers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: necessary to accomplish inspections and enforcement would achieve a different outcome than what existed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Fines cannot be imposed in the absence of inspections that are staffing dependent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Thus, I have no new testimony this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: I simply repeat and implore that no new unenforceable regulations are required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: Prevention is simply...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: dependent on performing inspections, monitoring compliance, and issuance of fines for noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Loftman
utterances.text: It's not my desire to be here again next year.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Appreciate your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to ask our President, President Brian O'Minn-Sigel, you walked in at the right time to give testimony.

chapters.summary: Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal reports 520 Manhattan buildings haven't reported cooling tower samples in two months, with 347 never reporting. He supports several bills and announces a Manhattan Legionnaires Disease Task Force of community board members.
chapters.title: Manhattan BP Hoylman-Sigal on cooling tower compliance gaps and task force

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I'm Brad Whilman, Siegel Manhattan Borough President.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I wanted to thank you and members of your committee and the Speaker for holding this important hearing,

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: which of course is on the Legionnaires disease outbreak and has largely been at least publicly focused on several neighborhoods in Manhattan, but we know that it is a five borough issue.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Madam Chair, I don't have to tell you that we know that Legionnaires disease has been increasing since the early 2000s.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: In 2025, as the CDC reported, New York City had the highest case rate in the country with 7.8 cases per 100,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And this year, for the second year in a row, Manhattan experienced a major cluster with 94 confirmed cases and, tragically, 11 known deaths.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And I know family members are here today, and I want to thank them for their testimony.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And no New Yorker should have to face this, so I'm very sorry for your losses.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: When the Upper East Side cluster was detected, DOHMH acted quickly, I think, testing and remediating cooling towers in the neighborhood within days.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Thankfully, the Upper East Side cluster is now contained.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And yet, we're here today with these family members, and it's past time we focus resources on prevention of this disease entirely, in addition to quick containment.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And as you well know, there are still many acts.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: active cases in the city.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: The general public most often learns of Legionnaires when cooling towers are contaminated, but there are also less public cases when Legionnaires is suspected to be spreading through a building's internal hot water system.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Through these instances, though they cause fewer Legionnaires cases than when cooling towers spread the bacteria through a community,

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: they are also serious public health concerns and can be very complicated to remediate and most often impact housing developments in underserved areas.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I've heard from many Manhattanites, and you have too today,

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: who fear for their health and safety and don't know what measures they need to take to reduce their risk of getting sick.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: We can and must do better, and I'm glad to see that the Council is considering this package of reforms to strengthen the City's response to this disease.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I strongly support your legislation, Madam Chair, Intro 1016, to create a DOHMH

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: run Legionnaires hotline.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I support Councilmember Hank's pre-considered legislation to improve regulation of cooling towers for buildings under construction.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I was glad to see Councilmember Ferraris'proposal, Intro 181, to require building owners to proactively offer shower hoses to all residents affected by

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: building investigations.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Finally, I urge DOHMH to consider ways to increase education and standardize outreach to residents.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: and impacted buildings and believe Councilmember Maloney's Intro 1005 will go a long way to aid those efforts.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: We know that the city already has laws in the books.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: After last year's Central Harlem Legionnaires Cluster, now new cooling tower reporting, testing, and maintenance requirements were passed by you here, which went into effect in May.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: These laws increase the frequency of testing and operational cooling towers from every three months to monthly and require a shock disinfection of cooling towers in the summer months.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: My office analyzed the 5,945 buildings with cooling tower systems registered citywide.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Manhattan alone accounts for almost 75% of the city's cooling towers, with 4,405 in the borough.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: But there are 520 buildings, Madam Chair, in the borough of Manhattan that have not reported a new sample in at least the last two months.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: The majority of these buildings, 347, have not reported any samplings at all.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: DOHMH, I think, should investigate whether these buildings are in violation and ensure swift and regular compliance across the city.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: The city has an obligation to ensure that there are staffing and resources available to implement these ends.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mayor Mondani, the Department of Health, and the Department of Buildings for their

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: announcement yesterday to strengthen enforcement of cooling tower regulations.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And I look forward to seeing those actions implemented.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: It's abundantly clear that Legionnaires will continue to impact New Yorkers for years to come, especially as the impacts of climate change continue to increase.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: As the weather warms,

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: We're going to need more cooling towers, as well as the fact that studies suggest warmer weather increases the incidence of the Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And we know that New Yorkers want to help, so I'm happy to announce that my office is in the early stages of creating a Manhattan Legionnaires Disease Task Force comprised of community board members in Manhattan to support and

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: improve communications to New Yorkers impacted by the disease.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I hope this group of stakeholders can serve as a resource in amplifying the public health messaging that is quick, transparent, and collaborative.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I want to thank you, Madam Chair, again for your leadership on this issue and so many issues of public health that affect all of us.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Board President.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: A question.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The ones that you said hadn't been...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Done in terms of the cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Have you told DOHMH that?

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: We have communicated that to them.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I would like to know what they respond back to you, and we would like to work with your office.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I would like to work with your office.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In terms of communication, there are some things that we've come up with out

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: side of this hearing that we thought might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So especially given the amount of cooling towers, the other is that

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have talked to some folks in the administration about the fact that we're going to, once we start building new housing, we've got to take a look at what we're doing with the cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I think that's important, especially in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And, of course, there's new technology to ward off Legionella.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That would be awesome.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But we have to do this collectively with everybody.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I thank you for your efforts and your commitment, and we look forward to working with you moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, now we have next panel.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Next panel is Melissa Barbour.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Samuel Alito.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Lydia Diana.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: David Hawkins and April McIver.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, as I've stated earlier, to the extent that you can keep your testimony to two minutes would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We have a lot of people that want to testify.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And you can certainly submit the testimony, and we're looking at everything, because this is obviously very important.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So we'll start over on this side.

chapters.summary: April McIver of the Plumbing Foundation urges shifting from reactive to proactive prevention, arguing the cooling tower focus is inadequate. She calls for reintroducing Intro 434 to mandate testing of entire building water systems and criticizes green building laws that promote bacteria growth.
chapters.title: April McIver of Plumbing Foundation calls for holistic water system testing

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I'm April McIver, Executive Director of the Plumbing Foundation, a nonprofit trade association representing the New York City licensed plumbing industry.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Our mission is to ensure the passage and enforcement of safe plumbing codes.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: First, I give my condolences to the families of the 11 who have lost their lives this summer from the recent outbreak.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: We are here today to demand a shift from reacting to Legionnaire's disease to proactively preventing it.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: While the city has hyper-focused on cooling towers since 2015, recent deadly outbreaks, including the 7 in Harlem last year and the 11 on the Upper East Side this year, prove this approach is severely inadequate.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: The bacteria is actively spreading through internal building water systems.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Speaker Menon mentioned the Haven Plaza today, and Councilmember Farias spoke about Parkchester.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: We want to look at this holistically, comprehensively.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: So potable water systems where New Yorkers shower, wash their hands, brush their teeth are a frequent source of Legionella exposure.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Furthermore, well-intentioned green building laws that lower hot water temperatures, promote low flow fixtures, and most recently, encourage the use of plastic piping and the mayor's block-by-block housing plan as an alternative

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: material, create the perfect breeding grounds for this deadly bacteria.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Our written testimony has comments on most of the legislation on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: today, which we explain as supporting, but with amendments to each of the bills.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I do want to bring us to our primary focus today, reintroduction of Intro 434 of 2024.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: We urgently call on the Council to reintroduce this bill with critical provisions restored as provided to the Council.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: We must mandate proactive maintenance and testing for entire building water systems.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: A truly comprehensive bill will require clear, strict standards and direct the Department of Health, as we know they are struggling with enforcement.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: A reintroduction of 434.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Finish.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: It's much longer.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I just very quickly like to say, you know, I have been working at this organization for nine years, working on this issue for seven years.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I have met so many, so many experts and people.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I'm an attorney, but I've spoken to so many people.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I read a lot.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: I do a lot of research.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: And I think New York City is really focusing this in a bubble in the cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: And I think we really do need to expand this and look at this holistically.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: More in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: April McIver
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Melissa Barber of the Mechanical Contractors Association supports Intro 1006 with amendments, urges studying chemical volumes to prevent corrosion, and calls for an advisory board with contractor representation to discuss energy code impacts on water stagnation.
chapters.title: Melissa Barber of MCA on chemical use and advisory panel

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Hi, thank you for the opportunity to testify at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Before I begin, I want to extend my sympathy to everyone affected by the recent outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: My name is Melissa Barber, and I'm the Assistant Director for the Mechanical Contractors Association of New York.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Our members install, service, test, repair, and maintain

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: maintain heating, ventilation, cooling, and air conditioning, refrigeration, and fire sprinkler systems throughout New York City and Long Island, employing Steamfitters Local 638 building trades and metal trades members to perform this work.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Collectively, we have over 250 contractors and 6,000 union members working daily on the central nervous systems of our city's building.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Our mechanical contractors, along with their water treatment subcontractors, are at the forefront of installing, testing, and maintaining new and existing cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: We offer the following testimony on this oversight hearing and corresponding bills.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: The regulations that began to be enforced this past spring were a correct step in addressing recent Legionnaires disease outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: However, this summer's outbreak shows that current requirements may warrant some further review.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: We support the intention of Intro 1006, and we have some minor language changes that we would like to submit for consideration.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: However, we also do believe that it's imperative that the city further study and review the volume and type of chemicals introduced into systems, particularly the amount of chlorine and bromine used.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: For example, excessive levels of these chemicals could cause...

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Piping corrosion and pitting, which are precisely the conditions in which Legionella thrives.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: So more is not always better.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: We also support Intro 1017, but we would also ask that the council develop an advisory board or panel that's part of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Our contractors are installing and servicing these systems day in and day out and can

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: offer unrivaled field experience and boots on the ground insight.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: One unintended consequence of more energy efficient buildings has been reduced water movement in cooling towers and often at lower velocity.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: This is a result of energy saving pumping reductions.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll make it quick.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Less frequent water or lower flow pumping can mean that water can sit longer.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Instead of properly circulating, which encourages biofilm buildup on walls.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: So in response, our contractors are already seeing a shift towards cooling tower and pump designs that run pumps faster to reduce stagnation, along with upgrades that reduce aerosolized water.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: As we all work to curb Legionnaire's disease outbreaks, discussions on the impact of energy code mandates, system redesigns, new technology, and remediation techniques should occur on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Finally, we urge the Council to ensure that all agencies have sufficient staff to fulfill city mandates.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: When agencies face limited workforce resources, communities are left at risk, and New York City must ensure that agencies providing vital public health and safety services can attract and retain staff and the staff levels required to do so.

utterances.speaker: Melissa Barber
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Samuel Aludo of the Building Trade Employers Association supports an advisory panel examining chemical use and green building mandates, urges adequate agency staffing, and supports reintroducing Intro 434 for comprehensive building water system testing.
chapters.title: Samuel Aludo of BTEA on advisory panel and building water system testing

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman, for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: My name is Samuel Aludo, member of Relations Director for the Building Trade Employers Association, former Council Member Elizabeth Crowley, President and CEO of the BTA.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Regret she couldn't be here today.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: The BTA is an umbrella organization of New York's construction industry, representing 24 member associations, more than 1,200 contractors who build and maintain New York's building and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: And today's testimony comes at a somber moment with 11 New Yorkers who lost their lives to Legionnaire's disease, and our recommendations are designed to make New Yorkers safer.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: First, we support MCA of New York's recommendation for an advisory board or panel, and we ask that they examine two things, the volume and types of chemicals introduced into these systems, particularly

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: chlorine and bromine, since excessive levels cause corrosion and pitting in which the disease thrives, and how also green building mandates from the city and state are contributing to the stagnation

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: of water, which creates biofilm and which never reached the temperatures needed to kill bacteria, and contractors should be on this panel.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Sometimes these kinds of boards leave off contractors, which is problematic.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Second, we urge the council to ensure agencies'staff fulfill the city mandates to conduct inspections, review registrations, and process sign-offs.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: New York City must ensure that age

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: He's providing vital public health and safety services can attract and retain the staff levels required to do so.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Third, we support the reintroduction of Intro 434 of 2024 to expand the testing of existing.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Cooling towers, but also the entire building's water system, where bacteria frequently grows.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Potable water is not currently tested, yet research has found that Legionella grows as well.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: It needs to be reviewed and inspected.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Any reintro of the bill should also carry amendments that I believe the Plumbing Foundation has laid out, including mandatory risk management assessments, addressing dead legs and stagnant water, a defined testing interval, and clear qualification standards.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you summarize?

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: I also support MCA's amendments on Intro 1006, which they've submitted as well.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: Samuel Aludo
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: David Hawkins of Operating Engineers Local 94 urges mandating water treatment training for cooling tower operators and proposes a DOHMH 7C Cooling Tower Operator Certification focused on Chapter 8 requirements and Legionella minimization.
chapters.title: David Hawkins of Local 94 on cooling tower operator certification

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Shulman.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: My name is David Hawkins, and I am the training director of the International Union of Operating Gears, Local 94.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Before I begin, I would like to send my union's condolences to the families of the people that passed away in the latest outbreak.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Local 94 represents approximately 7,000 members who work as engineers, help as fire persons throughout the New York City, serving in commercial buildings, hotels, New York City public schools, power plants, and a wide variety of other facilities.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Local 94 engineers are on the front lines of many safety-related mechanical issues in our city.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: They are no greater responsibilities than protecting the lives of our residents.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Local 94 represents some of the best trained stationary engineers in the country, and we are extensive training and first-hand experience operating and maintaining New York City's complex building systems.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Our members are uniquely positioned to assist the city in both the prevention and mitigation of Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Cooling tower water treatment is a complex issue and requires true partnership between city, building owners, engineers, and water treatment companies.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Because Legionella is prevalent in cooling towers and other building systems, the FDNY Refrigeration Machine Operators Q01 Certificate of Fitness Holders must receive the highest levels of education and training effectively to contain and prevent future outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: For this reason, Local 94 urges the city to mandate specific water treatment training for operation and maintenance of cooling towers and other building systems with Legionella.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Our recommendation to New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene create a streamlined version of the existing New York State 7G certification rebranded as DOHA 7C Cooling Tower Operator Certification.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: The certificate would focus on new requirements under Chapter 8, which require building owners with cooling towers to collect and report dates of Legionella samples at least monthly, as well as proper oversight and administration of cooling tower maintenance as it relates to minimizing the presence of Legionella.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: The CTOC will also focus on a responsible person's role that is outlined in Chapter 8 cooling tower rules.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: Education on these requirements is essential and success that Chapter 8 and safety of our citizens in New York City.

utterances.speaker: David Hawkins
utterances.text: This additional certification should be

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman

chapters.summary: Lydia Diana of the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council describes the Highline Hotel's Legionella contamination where management didn't notify workers, follow-up tests showed fourfold increase, and workers faced retaliation for safety concerns. She calls for a worker hotline and enforcement measures.
chapters.title: Lydia Diana of Hotel Trades Council on Highline Hotel worker exposure

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: I want to thank the council members this morning, as well as thank you, Chair Shulman, for a convenient oversight hearing on the city's response to this summer's Legionnaire outbreak.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: My name is Lydia Diana, and I am an organizer with the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council Union.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: I have spent over a decade committed to ensuring hardworking hotel workers are guaranteed the wages, safety, and dignity they deserve, as well as a voice, and that's why I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: I represent the workers at the Highline Hotel, a luxury property right in downtown Manhattan, operated by MCR.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Earlier this summer, the hotel building received a test showing higher than average rates of the Legionella bacteria cooling towers on the property.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Management did not notify the union or the workers and refused to provide evidence that they were following the law until after the union took them to arbitration.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: However, even after taking the steps required by law, follow-up tests two weeks later showed that the Legionella density had increased fourfold.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Under New York City law, 10 colonial forming units per milliliter is considered acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: An immediate action in reporting to the city is only required if the rates exceed 1,000 CFU.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Rates at the Highline Hotel after management first remediated it over 700.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Because it was below that red line threshold, the law only requires that the building either increase or change the chemicals in the system and to perform a visual inspection.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: There was nothing else the city could do.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: With the current response in place, workers and guests were left uninformed and vulnerable to the potential health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Management tried to keep business running as usual.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Workers with pre-existing respiratory conditions or weakened immune systems were threatened with retaliation when they expressed concerns over their safety.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Just summarize to the extent that you can.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: It's critical to maintain strict standards.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: We want to keep building a world's number one tourist destination in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: So thankfully, no one got sick.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: The lack of proper oversight and enforcement mechanisms to keep workers and guests informed and healthy were inadequate.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: We have learned time and time again that the Legionnaire is not an issue to take lightly and delay in action.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: Solutions, we suggest, like a hotline for workers to voice concerns without fear of retaliation, enforcement,

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: measures to hold non-compliant businesses accountable will significantly help keep workers and guests safe.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: I implore this city to reform its protocols and make sure responsible parties are held accountable when health and safety standards are not adhered to.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: The risk is too high not to.

utterances.speaker: Lydia Diana
utterances.text: I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I also, you may know this, I worked with Megan on this too.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: She had called me when that first happened.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I want to thank everyone here for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It's really important.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And please tell Elizabeth I said hello.
